## S: shoeman–Spanish windlass

### shoeman

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  A mutual agreement has been entered into by the Sawmillers' Society and employers, under which a week's work is fixed at 48 hours, and the minimum wages as follows:- .. bushmen, shoemen, trollymen [sic], and stokers, 9s; ... <i>(May 28, 1901,Taranaki Herald,2</i>)

>  <b>BREMER</b> The man accompanying the logs to the hauler was known as a shoeman and he generally had a whistle boy who stopped the hauler by means of a whistle when the log reached one of the snatch blocks. <i>(1983,Port Craig,5</i>)

>  <b>IVAN BANNISTER</b> In logging to the mill skids the man who puts the shoe over the nose of the log to save sniping. <i>(May 1985,Personal Communication</i>)

>  <b>BIRD</b> The shoeman had the least desirable job of any in the bush. His job was to follow the log along the haul track back to the engine. <i>(1998,Viaducts against the Sky,65</i>)

<i>verb</i>. -

[NOTES: ca1945 Wellington University Undergrads and Training College students.]

>  <b>WILSON</b> He shogged along with a shambling, limping shuffle, <i>(1984,South Pacific Street,27</i>)

### shog off

 
<i>exclamation</i>. be off! occas used in NZ, and felt to be a humorous variant of shag v.

[NOTES: ca1934 Dunedin. A. Campbell -]

<i>noun</i>.

>  The good ship Aiuckland will soon be back on course to a future of shoddy shonk built on the rubble of a shady past. <i>(Jun 27, 2004,Sunday Star Times,A11</i>)

<i>noun</i>.

### shonky

>  After a lot of rummaging, he finds a shonky corkscrew, a couple of glasses and a cup. <i>(Oct 19, 2002,Listener (New Zealand Listener),33</i>)

### shoof

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a protective shoe for hooves of cattle and sheep.

>  The Shoof is manufactured in five sizes to fit a range of animals from small cattle through to medium sized horses. <i>(May 1981,NZ Journal of Agriculture,74</i>)

>  Journal readers will already be familiar with the 'shoof' shoes, designed to protect bandages on the hooves of horses and cattle. One model of interest is the elevated cattle shoof, which is built up on either the right or left side. Shoofs are made from strong urethane material and should last 3 to 6 months if they're used continuously. <i>(May 1982,NZ Journal of Agriculture,11</i>)

>  Shoof - a shoe for a hoof - protects and treats damaged hooves. <i>(Jun 1982,NZ Dairy Exporter,41</i>)

### shook

 
<i>adjective</i>. uncertain; unsound; unwell

[NOTES: ca1935 egs I feel pretty shook about her. None of us knows what she is. It's a pretty shook scheme they're hatching up. I always feel shook half way across the Straits.]



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  landed 100 Cask and shooks on the beach <i>(Feb 20, 1836,Piraki Log,28,ed. Anson 1911</i>)

>  <b>CAPT. JOY</b> heavy wind at SE and Whirlwinds [at Cloudy Bay] Cleared decks Setting up shooks <i>(May 4, 1836,Log of Mary Mitchell</i>) [NOTES: 1836 May 4 Capt. Joy <i>Mary Mitchell</i> log in 1913 McNab Old Whaling Days 439]



 
<i>adjective</i>. shook up

>  <b>VIRTUE</b> He thought she might be a bit shook about Aunt Melva, who was crook. <i>(1987,Redemption of Elsdon Bird, The,4,1988</i>)

### shook on

 
<i>phrase</i>. keen on; having a crush on

>  I'm quite "shook" on what I've seen of the Grand Old Country. <i>(Jul 11, 1918,Wanganui Herald,4</i>)

>  I later learned this mainly meant that Morrieson put away a power of drink, and was a bit too shook on Maoris. <i>(Jun 12, 1982,Listener (New Zealand Listener),100</i>)

>  <b>WOOD</b> That cousin of her's is awfully shook on her. <i>(1875,Waiting for the Mail,80</i>)

>  You may be dead shook on the girl, but that doesn't give you license [sic] to gently bite her ear as you go spinning round, well upon the toes, in a merry waltz. <i>(Nov 28, 1908,NZ Truth,180/1/4</i>)

>  `Alan's a bit shook on Miss Lestrange, isn't he, mother?' `It begins to look like it, I must say.' `And what about her? Funny he's never had a girl before.' <i>(Jul 10, 1915,Triad, The,415</i>)

>  <b>ANTHONY</b> Nobody but a durn fool ever discusses a girl with a man that is shook on her. <i>(1924,Follow the Call,34,1975</i>)

>  <b>DEVANNY</b> The state of mind described by girls as being `shook' on a man <i>(1926,Butcher Shop, The,43</i>)

>  <b>ANTHONY</b> I can't say I was shook on Gus's style. <i>(1937,Me and Gus,73,1977</i>) [NOTES: Gus Tomlins ed. Sturm]

>  <b>DEVANNY</b> All the girls were shook on him. <i>(1928,Dawn Beloved,110</i>)

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> Now don't say that about my tin plate or I'll go crook: He is out on his own and, in fact, he is shook on me. <i>(1935,Slang Today,287</i>) [NOTES: 1935 A.E. Strong WW1 scene in Partridge Slang Today 287]

>  <b>MARSH</b> What they used to call `shook on the pros' .... He hangs around Carolyn [the star actress]. <i>(1937,Vintage Murder,9</i>)

>  <i>shook on adj. (Sl.)</i> in love with <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18</i>)

>  <i>shook on NZ & Austral. colloq</i>. keen on or infatuated by. <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,706</i>) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]



 
<i>adjective</i>. keen on, taken with

[NOTES: (with negative as below is the most common form of the idiom in NZ)]

>  <b>CADEY</b> If you find you're not too shook on it up there.. just come along and look us up. <i>(1933,Broken Pattern,95</i>)

>  <i>Shook on, to be</i>.-To admire, to be keen on, e.g., `I'm not so <i>s.o.</i> his horse.' <i>(Jan 27, 1934,Press, The,15</i>)

>  <b>SARGESON</b> He wasn't shook on women anyhow. <i>(1936,Conversations with My Uncle,26</i>) [NOTES: (`I`ve lost my girl')]

>  <b>SARGESON</b> shook: <i>wasn't too shook on</i>, wasn't keen on. <i>(1964,Collected Stories,303</i>)

>  <b>SHADBOLT</b> `Still not too keen on it, are you?' `On what?' `The bush. Still not too bloody shook on it, are you? I can tell.' <i>(1965,Among the Cinders,209</i>)

>  <b>SLATTER</b> Not too shook on him at all - The selector had a snitch on me - <i>(1968,Pagan Game, The,164</i>)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>shook on </i>very keen on person or thing; eg `I can't say I'm much shook on a guy who marches in as if he owns the place.' NZA. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,101</i>)

### shoot

 
<i>verb</i>.

>  <b>McCARTHY</b> The same thing applied after the face had been `shot': before shovelling (or bogging, as it was called) the stone down the pass it had to be thoroughly drenched with water ... <i>(1973,Listen...!,51</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  [Two] other pannikins were placed in the `<i>shoot</i>', the coldest part of the freezing apparatus [of a ship]. <i>(1883,TrNZI</i>) [NOTES: (Heath)]



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <i>Shoot.</i>- ... (2) Narrow, newly formed watercourse with very hard, steep sides. A shepherd's word. They sometimes call it a <i>shoot</i>. [Sometimes, a <i>guts</i>.--A.W.] <i>(1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]



 
<i>noun</i>. a precipitous rock face

>  <b>CHAMIER</b> He told him to mind the siding by the shoot [when driving his dray] <i>(1891,Philosopher Dick,360</i>)

>  <b>GUTHRIE-SMITH</b> We led our horses over the `shoot', the almost perpendicular drop, down which the pack-team used in muddy weather to slide with stiff legs and unlifted hoofs. <i>(1926,Tutira,148</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>.

>  <b>THOMPSON</b> A party that was shooting the nearby country also used it as a base. <i>(1952,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,66</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

See: chute

>  The dredged material falls into a shoot which carries it into a revolving cylinder ... <i>(1887,Handbook NZ Mines,40</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  The rich shoot of ore did not continue down <i>(1906,NZ Mining Handbook,44</i>)

<i>phrase</i>. [Rural] to go duck-shooting.

>  <b>STACEY</b> Jack Bugler .. had arranged to shoot a dam during the shooting season. <i>(1996,Tales of a Tussock Jumper,151</i>)

### shoot in

 
<i>verb</i>. to run in, put in jail (esp. in passive: get shot in)

>  How we saw that day out without getting `shot in' is a mystery to me yet. <i>(1947,Wayleggo,38</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> [He] had nearly got `shot in' for getting into a drunken argument with a fishmonger. <i>(1949,High Country Days,14</i>)

>  More care should be taken by the police in shooting in people for making themselves offensive in a public place. On May 4, five persons were charged but, ... , the fines were smaller than usual. <i>(May 14, 1910,NZ Truth,255/7/2</i>)

>  No disorder prevailed, and the drunk was locked up in a cell till he would be sober enough to release. The disgrace attending the circumstance of a highly-respectable citizen being `shot in' for shikkur was felt by other leading respectable members of Dannevirke community, and endeavours were made to influence the local sergeant of police to release the drunk. <i>(Jan 28, 1911,NZ Truth,292/6/6</i>)

### shoot off

 
<i>verb</i>. to go, leave

>  <b>SHADBOLT</b> ' ... I think I'll just potter round here quietly by myself the rest of the day. ... You two shoot off.' <i>(1965,Among the Cinders,170</i>)

>  <b>MCG</b> <i> shoot off/through</i> leave suddenly or improperly; eg `Todd, we have to shoot through, mate. Sorry, ta-ta.' NZA. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,101</i>)

### shoot one's bolt

 
<i>phrase</i>. to do one's dash, to do all one can to a point of collapse (general English); also in sexual sense to ejaculate

>  <b>FULLARTON</b> I reckon I've shot my bolt. This arm's giving me merry hell. <i>(1944,Troop Target,86</i>)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>shoot one's bolt </i>male ejaculation, often premature, or to have given one's best and/or all; eg `Ben's shot his bolt this round.' NZA. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,101</i>)

### shoot over

 
<i>verb</i>.

>  <b>THOMSON</b> After five months of shooting, we returned once more to the Albertburn to commence shooting over the block again. <i>Ibid.</i> 85 ..., we would shoot nearby branch valleys that could be shot over in the hours we had to spare between the morning and evening shoot. <i>(1952,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,75</i>)

### shoot through on

>  <b>CRUMP</b> He'd probably never miss the Old Girl if he shot through on her. <i>Ibid.</i> 190 What'd y' do, Sam? Shoot through on `im? <i>(1961,Hang on a Minute, Mate,11</i>)

>  <b>WATSON</b> to desert ... that's what I come [sic] all the way up here for, to get me old mate Tommy, he wouldn't shoot through on a man. <i>(1965,Stand in the Rain,57</i>)

### shoot up like a gum tree

>  <b>CHAMIER</b> A youngster that has shot up like a gum tree <i>(1891,Philosopher Dick,184</i>)

### shooter

 
<i>noun</i>. a marble

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as `taw' or `shooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; `dubs', `dates', `stakes', `dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,174</i>)

### shooting block

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] an area of bush or back-country allocated to hunters and cullers by the Forestry Service.

>  <b>THOMSON</b> Ron, the packman, left us early next morning to continue packing other parties to their shooting blocks. <i>(1952,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,70</i>)

>  <b>THOMSON</b> ... they wouldn't unduly interefere with our shooting block, otherwise I was to send them 'down the track.' <i>(1964,Deer Shooting Days,81</i>)

>  <b>MCCONOCHIE</b> Next morning Selwyn and I returned to our shooting block in Cow Valley. <i>(1966,You'll Learn No Harm from the Hills,133</i>)

>  <b>HOLDEN</b> .. he had found himself turning increasingly to the wilderness as an alternative means of making a living - possum hunting in the winter and transporting hunters in his boats to the various 'shooting blocks' across the lake at almost any time of the year. <i>(1996,Great Hunting Yarns,70</i>)

### shooting camp

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a temporary camp of cullers or rabbiters in the high country.

>  Curiosity being aroused, I ... found that during the shooting season of the last year (1893) a young man of Dannevirke ...out shooting, had there seen a taniwha (unknown watery monster), and had fired at it and wounded it. <i>(1895,TrNZI,28/87</i>)

### short tussock

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  Less grand and altogether less fortunate are the short tussocks. Growing up to half a metre in height, they include such hardy species as blue tussock (<i>Poa colensoi</i>), silver tussock (<i>P. cita</i>) and hard, or fescue, tussock (<i>Festuca novaezelandiae</i>. With a penchant for lower country, short tussocks have had to compete over the last 200 years with the runholder's arsenal of fire, exotic grases and grazing stock, and also wih the runholder's enemies - weeds and rabbits. [29] While the grass family is most likely to have originated in South America, our short tussocks appear to have arisen from ancestors that moved to, and diversified in, the northern hemisphere and then trickled back south. ... Short tussocks migrated up-slope from dry valley bottoms to meet them. <i>(Nov 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 66/28</i>)

### shortjaw kokopu

 
<i>noun</i>.

[NOTES: also shortjawed kokopu.]

>  The shortjaw kokopu is one of five native fish species commonly referred to as whitebait when they are juveniles migrating back to fresh water. Two of these species are classified as endangered, with a similar threat classification as eastern falcon, kereru and great spotted kiwi ... <i>(Aug 28, 2008,Dominion Post,B5</i>)

>  <b>McDOWALL</b> The fifth species is the rarest of all. It is the shortjawed kokopu (<i>Galaxias postvectis</i>), a species that is also rare as an adult. <i>Ibid.</i> 50 Shortjawed kokopu behave similarly to banded kokopu. They also climb falls and move well inland... Most shortjawed kokopu are found in small streams in unmodified native forest, usually in pools with thick cover,especially where there are piles of logs or boulders among which the fish can hide. <i>(1984,NZ Whitebait Book, The,14</i>)

>  <b>PAUL</b> Shortjawed kokopu Galaxias postvectis Widely distributed but localised, secretive and seldom seen. <i>(1986,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,48</i>)

>  Several shortjaw kokopu, a nationally threatened species, were found in the lower reaches of the stream. <i>(Jan 25, 2005,Independent Herald (Wellington),9</i>)

>  On the West Coast, the season runs from September 1 till November 14 to improve the minor late-running species' chance of reaching coastal wetlands for giant kokopu, or forest-covered streams for short-jawed and banded kokopu, and koaro. <i>(Nov 11, 2003,Dominion Post,A18</i>)

>  The short-jaw kokopu usually grows to about 20 centimetres and lives in streams with native forest cover. <i>(Aug 26, 2006,Dominion Post,E7</i>)

>  Inanga are the most common species, but whitebaiters may also capture the young of giant kokopu, koaro and banded kokopu. "Shortjaw and giant kokopu are described as threatened species. ..." <i>(Aug 17, 2005,Whakatane Beacon,4</i>)

>  <b>DENNIS</b> The juveniles of five species of galaxias make up the whitebait catch: inanga (<i>Galaxias maculatus</i>), koaro (<i>G. brevipinnis</i>), banded kokopu (<i>G. fasciatus</i>), giant kokopu (<i>G. argenteus</i>) and short-jawed kokopu (<i>G. postvectis>/i>). -- <i>(1981,Paparoas Guide,187</i>)</i>

>  The sarge wandered past with a shotty in each hand on his way to one of the marked police cars parked out front, where he opened the boot to secure the weapons and ammunition. <i>(2007,Best New Zealand Fiction, Vol 4, The,39</i>) [NOTES: 'The Good and the Gentle', Ben Brown, 2007]

>  The shotties were loaded and they weren't there just for effect. <i>(2007,Best New Zealand Fiction, Vol 4, The,36</i>) [NOTES: 'The Good and the Gentle', Ben Brown, 2007]

>  <b>MCGILL</b> shotty: shotgun, among hunters. <i>(1989,Dinkum Kiwi Dictionary, The,94</i>)

>  <b>KERR</b> She got the shotty, rammed two shells home, went out, lined up on the rabbit, closed her eyes, pulled the trigger and blew Bugs into history ... <i>(2000,High Times in the High Country,96</i>)

>  rifle or shotgun - a shotty. <i>(2001,Questionnaire Respondents (DB)</i>)

>  <b>BATTYE & EAKIN</b> He set his trap and sat down to wait behind a tree -/ with his shottie in his hand. <i>Ibid.</i> 72 shottie <i>shot-gun </i> <i>(1980,Shadow of the Valley,41</i>)

### shotty

 
<i>adjective</i>.

>  We, however, extended our researches farther up the river as well as down the gorge; the gold up the river was round and shotty, and in the gorge, although more scaly, was abundant, and Mr. Stone is of opinion this part of the river will pay well in summer. <i>(Nov 14, 1857,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,3</i>)

>  ... the general character of the gold being scaly and fine, the reverse of shotty, but some of the nuggets are quite waterworn and solid. <i>(Sep 27, 1861,NZ Goldfields,29,1976</i>) [NOTES: 1861 Sep 27 Tuapeka in NZ Goldfields 1861 (1976) 29]

>   <i>(May 20, 1869,Letter</i>) [NOTES: 1869 May 20 letter in1962 Evans Waikaka Saga 16]

>  <b>HOGG</b> 'Twas when the Rocky River rush began/ ... `and stories told/ Of ounces gotten in a single pan,/ Of nuggety, and round, and shotty gold./ The news like a bush fire through the diggings ran,/ <i>(1875,Lays and Rhymes,176</i>)

>  The gold was heavy and shotty. <i>(1887,Handbook NZ Mines,130</i>)

>  Gold is from fine to shotty. <i>(1906,Mining Handbook,134</i>)

>  <b>AYSON</b> The result was that in a few afternoons he had filled a tin matchbox with coarse, shotty gold. <i>(1937,Thomas,29</i>)

>  <b>SUTHERLAND</b> Smooth, worn gold lay together with coarse, `shotty' and rough-sided pieces [47] which could not have travelled far through alluvial action. <i>(1953,Golden Bush, The,46</i>)

>  <b>SUTHERLAND</b> There was nothing very big but it was chunky and rough, `shotty' as the diggings called it, and there was almost no fine gold in the wash, which made catching easy. <i>(1953,Golden Bush, The,119,1963</i>)

>  <b>MAY</b> The gold was shotty and coarse compared with the fine, flaky deposits of Waimea and Kaniere; <i>(1967,West Coast Gold Rushes,161,1962</i>)

>  <b>WOOD</b> Crevicing can be a fascinating occupation, for one never knows when one might find a virgin crevice with its quota of shotty gold and even a small nugget. <i>(1970,Gold Trails of Otago,81</i>)

>  shotty gold hard, round pieces of gold <i>(1984,Blackball 08,245</i>)

### shotty gold

 
<i>noun</i>. alluvial gold in a pellet form resembling gunshot

>  It is shotty, not flaky gold, that is theDiggers Delight. <i>(Feb 9, 1924,Grey River Argus,7</i>)

>  I have just seen, in possession of a storekeeper, nearly 50 ounces of splendid shotty gold obtained from the Quartz Ranges, being decidedly the best general sample yet, which I've no doubt will be a great inducement to many to "try thier [sic] luck" there, now that there is something like a decent track to that quarter. <i>(Dec 12, 1857,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,3</i>)

>  From Torrie Bros.' claim, Cardrona,  there is a sample of coarse shotty gold. <i>(Mar 6, 1890,Otago Witness,19</i>)

### shoulda shot that horse

 
<i>phrase</i>.

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>shoulda shot that horse</i> comment on bad booze, usually after first sip, especially of home brew. <i>[Jim Henderson] </i> <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,102</i>)

### shoulder

 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [sheepdogs] to tuck in the wings or flanks of a mob of sheep.

>  <b>WHYTE</b> Shouldering, or keeping in the flanks of a mob of sheep, is a very useful quality and one that every sheepdog should be taught. <i>(1927,Shepherd's Dogs, The,148</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [sheepdogs] to worry or force an individual sheep to move by working at its shoulder.

>  <b>WHYTE</b> Shouldering sheep is a bad fault. <i>(1927,Sheep-Dog, The,50</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [sheep] to temporarily dislocate a shoulder after jumping from an inappropriate height on a bank etc.

>  <b>MILLS ET AL</b> .. you should refrain from running a noisy dog on the top side of the mob, forcing the sheep to jump off banks down on to road or track, for sheep can 'shoulder' themselves very easily if they do this. <i>(1964,Practical Guide to Handling Dogs and Stock,87</i>)

### shoulder hole

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>McARA</b> The usual method of drilling was to start with the right-hand lifter, then the centre lifter, next the bottom right-hand cut hole, the knee hole, the stab (to break the outer part of the face and assist the cut) the bottom cut easer, then the hip hole, the right-hand cut easer, the two shoulder holes, the top right-hand cut hole, the top easer, the centre and right-hand back holes. <i>(1978,Gold Mining at Waihi,189</i>)

### shoulder one's swag

 
<i>phrase</i>. [Rural] to set out with one's belongings.

>  At 4 o'clock we most reluctantly shouldered the swag again, and retired to the foot of the hill. <i>(Feb 28, 1889,Otago Witness,2</i>)

>  We have this from a veracious traveller among the haunts of the Lost Tribe, who assures us that men have been coming back from the places named and have shouldered swag, pick, and shovel, and gone up the country to delve for the precious metal in the ground they had, some of them, abandoned years ago. <i>(Aug 10, 1893,West Coast Times,2</i>)

>  However, the five shouldered their swag. Humping their 'bluey" in this case was a matter of donning a bowler hat, brushing their English clothes, and shouldering each a large portmanteau. <i>(Feb 28, 1908,Wanganui Herald,7</i>)

>  <b>CHINN</b> The shearing was in full swing and those who had not been fortunate enough to obtain employment shouldered their swag and took to the road again. <i>(1963,Packtrack to Highway,62</i>)

### shoulder patch

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a kempy area on the back of a sheep's fleece between the neck and the centre back.

>  <b>BLACK & DYSON</b> Heterozygous lambs usually have fewer halo-hairs just behind the shoulder on the "shoulder-patch." <i>(1978,Carpetmakers: Specialty Carpet Wool breeds of NZ,5</i>)

>  <b>BLACK & DYSON</b> Whether the ewe is polled or horned helps to determine her genetic make-up, along with the presence or absence of a "shoulder patch." Check Drydale lambs at docking to see if they are NN or Nn by looking at the shoulder patch ... <i>(1978,Carpetmakers: Specialty Carpet Wool breeds of NZ,7</i>)

### shoulder roll

 
<i>noun</i>. [Science] a style or method of rolling a wool fleece, where after folding, the fleece is rolled from one end only.

>  <b>BOWEN</b> .. the following suggested shoulder-roll usually presents a fleece to better advantage ... This shoulder roll is simple and fast ... [shoulder roll] <i>(1955,Wool Away!,94</i>)

>  <b>BOWEN</b> [ST] THE SHOULDER ROLL When the fleece is skirted, turn one side in by one-third (i.e. one-third of the overall width of the fleece). Now fold again to meet the opposite edge of the fleece. The folded fleece is now rolled from one end, ... <i>(1955,Wool Away!,94</i>)

### shouldering

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>GORDON</b> <i>Shouldering:</i> a right or left <i>shoulder-man. </i> <i>(May 17, 1951,Personal Communication</i>) [NOTES: Feilding Freezing Works terms]



 
<i>noun</i>. (of a dog) ?stopping before it gets to the head of a mob to hold the sheep together

>  <b>LILICO</b> Another useful thing in working mobs is `shouldering' or `edging' as they used to call it on the Borders in my time [ca. 1870's] <i>(1934,Sheep Dog Memoirs,30</i>)

### shoulderman

 
<i>noun</i>. freezing worker

>  <b>HENDERSON</b> SHOULDERMEN (Knife only) <i>(1975,Log of a Superfluous Son, The,42</i>)

### shouse

 
<i>noun</i>. a euphemistic abbrev. of shithouse (cf. ted, as an abbrev. nickname from shithead) [AND 1941 B]

>  <b>SLATTER</b> He had heard a shoush rumour that they were going down to Trasimeno. <i>(1968,Pagan Game, The,71</i>)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>shouse</i> something very bad; contraction of `shithouse'; eg `It's total shouse out there, why not wait until it eases, eh?' <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,102</i>)

### shout

 
<i>verb</i>. v.i. often constr <i>for</i> (a person), to stand treat

>  On Monday 2nd Feb 1998, Peter Balance and Jack Grant-Mackie shouted a healthy morning tea for the geology staff and graduate students at Auckland University ... <i>(Mar 1998,Geological Society of NZ Newsletter,115/35</i>)

>  We took it into an hotel, shouted a drink to a loafer, and demanded his opinion on it. <i>(Mar 16, 1872,West Coast Times,2</i>)

>  Walsh called for drinks twice and paid for them, and James M'Rory also "shouted." <i>(Mar 30, 1888,Otago Witness,16</i>)

>  In the judgement, in the course of what he calls "the facts briefly," the Magistrate says that outside of the Newtown Hotel Routh "met an acquaintance whom he asked to shout; that the two went in together, and the acquaintance (Mulqueeny) did shout; and that Routh also asked the barman to shout, which the barman did." <i>(Sep 13, 1904,Evening Post,6</i>)

>  The supposed digger.. "shouted" champagne <i>ad lib.</i> <i>(Nov 14, 1855,Nelson Examiner,2</i>)

>  They [Titokowaru's followers] good-humouredly said it was their first visit to the surveyors, and that they expected some one to "shout". A bottle of whiskey was found and handed to them. <i>(1879,AJHR,C-4/12</i>)

>  If they cannot get anyone to "shout" for them, they ask for money. <i>(Nov 28, 1885,Wairarapa Daily,2</i>)

>  <b>BAXTER</b> Gandhi ... insisted on shouting seven dog's-noses for Horse in the bar of ther Shamrock. <i>(1962,Horse,83</i>) [NOTES: (Bulls and Cows)]

>  Claridge shouted him another whisky. <i>(May 16, 1934,NZ Truth,15</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> ... to say nothing of the fact that the first person in New Zealand to `shout' for me, which here means to ask you into a house of call and stand treat, should be the great Bishop! <i>(Dec 25, 1856,Letters from Canterbury, NZ,10,1914</i>)

>  <b>PYKE</b> And when Harry faintly avowed his ability to discharge all obligations, the `fiver' was recklessly expended by its owner in `Shouting for all hands'. <i>(1873,Wild Will Enderby,1/vii/28</i>)

>  <b>THATCHER</b> With an ovation she [the accused found not guilty] is now led out/ And for her every one desires <i>to shout. </i> <i>(1864,Invercargill Minstrel,4,1889. 1874</i>) [NOTES: (The Sessions) [a pun]]

>  <b>'J.K.M.'</b> Be them two outside your friends ? Have'm in and shout (treat) for'm. <i>(1867,Mary Ira,9</i>)

>  If the girls went to bed at twelve o'clock when [bar-room] dancing was over, they would be `growled' at by Mrs Crawford if there were men about the bar `shouting'. <i>(Jan 23, 1869,Grey River Argus,2</i>)

>  <b>BATHGATE</b> [Diggers] `shout for all hands' (ie., treat everyone in the house to drink). <i>(1874,Colonial Experiences,90</i>)

>  <b>WOOD</b> Are you off? Well, we'll look into Jones's,/ For I am going to shout./ <i>Ibid.</i>  79 `A' right, ...; will you shout if she comes?' `Yes, I'll shout.' <i>(1875,Waiting for the Mail,41</i>)

>  <b>BROOMHALL</b> The Colony is not free from slang, any more than the mother country. When at the Bay of Islands a native asked me to `shout' him, I thought him mad. He saw my difficulty and vociferated, `a pint of beer! a pint of beer!' My guide explained that to `shout' a man is `to stand treat'. <i>(1877,Journey in NZ,41</i>)

>  <b>BATHGATE</b> But though the doctor got the credit, ... of never refusing a drink and seldom `shouting', he on this occasion was steadfast in his refusal, ... <i>(1881,Waitaruna,220</i>)

>  <b>DAVIDSON</b> From tricks at cards, the fun changed to `a bob in' the winner shouting. <i>(1889,Stories of NZ Life,5</i>)

>  <b>DAVIDSON</b> ... Westall did sample this same whisky ... in company with Davie, for whom he `shouted' as soon as he reached the house [sc. hotel]. <i>(1889,In the Shadow of the Bush,33</i>)

>  <i>Shout, n.</i> to stand treat. (1) Of drink. (2) By transference, of other things. The successful digger used to <i>call</i> passers-by to drink at his expense. The origin may also be from noisy bar-rooms, or crowded bar-parlours, where the man who was to pay for the liquor or refreshment called or <i>shouted</i> for the waiter or barman. When many men drink together the waiter of course looks for payment for the man who first calls or shouts out for him to give him the order. Or is `pay the shout' a variant of `pay the shot,' or tavern reckoning? In its first sense the word has reached the United States, and is freely employed there. [1859] <i>(1898,Austral English,416</i>)

>  The few citizens [of Okarito] spend their time shouting for each other. <i>(1957,Mr Explorer Douglas,18</i>) [NOTES: [MS. I.T.G.] (1890s)]

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> I bet our guns will lay it down thick and heavy, and if I get out of the smack-up with a whole skin I will shout for all hands. <i>(1935,Slang Today,287</i>)

>  <b>TAYLOR</b> Had three double brandies and shouted a round for all the others which set me back considerably more than I had bargained for. <i>(1971,Plekhov Place, The,132</i>)

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> <i>Shout.</i> v. To stand drinks to the company, hence to even one person: v.i., 1859, H. Kingsley; v.t. to pay for drinks for (a person, persons), hence for (say) `smokes', 1867, Lindsay Gordon; hence, late C. 19-20, to entertain (a person, persons). Australian, hence New Zealand; by 1864-witness H., 3rd ed.-well-known in England. (Morris; O.E.D.) Ex shouting to the waiter to fetch drinks <i>(1937,Dictionary of Slang,764</i>)

>  <b>BENNETT</b> <i>to shout</i> is, specifically, to `stand a drink' ... but it now also means to treat another person, no matter what the place or occasion. <i>(1943,English as it is spoken in NZ,89</i>)

>  <b>STRONACH</b> Then - the old, old custom - he took us over to the hotel and [69] shouted for us. If he had offered us half a crown each we should have felt terribly insulted; it he had not shouted for us we should have felt the same! <i>(1953,Musterer on Molesworth,68</i>)

>  <b>FRAME</b>  <i>(1957,Owls Do Cry,47</i>) [NOTES: [check quot and usage]]

>  <b>HILLIARD</b> As Arthur pushed to the door the Samoan girl thrust her face into his and demanded, `Aincha gonna shout?' <i>(1960,Maori Girl,233</i>)

>  <b>D'AVIGDOR</b> The chap would hang about till some digger would <i>shout</i> to all comers. [fn] Shout: Colonial for offering drinks. <i>(1888,Antipodean Notes,48</i>)

>  We have seen boys encouraged by their elders to think it manly to "shout" and to drink at bars they may pass on their journeys. <i>(Dec 31, 1863,Lyttelton Times,4</i>)

>  He had wanted to "shout" for a friend of  his, a member of the orchestra. <i>(Jan 20, 1940,Otago Daily Times,17</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. (Also to treat (a person))

>  <b>DILKE</b> At every halt one or other of the passengers is expected to `shout', or `stand', as it would be called at home, `drinks all round' `What'll yer shout?' is the only question. <i>(1868,Greater Britain,1/339</i>)

>  <b>BROOMHALL</b>  <i>(1877,Journey in NZ,41</i>) [NOTES: see 1 above]

>  <b>SOLJAK</b> Following are examples of colloquialisms common to New Zealand and Australian English, with their English or American equivalent ... <i>shout:</i> treat; e.g. <i>I'll shout you to a drink </i> <i>(1946,New Zealand (various authors/titles),115</i>)

>  <b>GASKELL</b> In I goes and he shouts me a couple. <i>(1947,Big Game,23</i>)

>  <i>~ v.t.</i> to treat; to stand some one a drink;-n. payment for a drink or round of drinks. <i>(1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,10</i>)

>   <i>(1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),366</i>)

>  <b>McLINTOCK</b> Australian importations include ... to shout, to pay for another's drink,. . . <i>(1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,2/680</i>) [NOTES: Wall NZ Speech]



 
<i>verb</i>.

>  <i>Shout</i> - buy something for someone (often a drink). <i>(1944,US War Dept. Short Guide to NZ,39</i>)

>  <b>McLAGLAN</b> ... she shouted the two elder teenage boys a trip to Wellington. <i>(1965,Stethoscope & Saddlebags,184</i>)

>  <b>GRUNDY</b> At Christmas, George had shouted me a call home to my family ... <i>(1968,Who'd Marry a Doctor?,90</i>)

>  <i>shout v.</i> treat to liquor, gift or benefit, particularly to buy liquor for others in company. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),17</i>)

>  <i>shout ... 5. (tr.) Austral. & N.Z. inf.</i> to treat (someone) to (something), esp. a round of drinks. <i>(1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1068</i>) [NOTES: [1986 NZPOD 708; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 449]]

>  His wife had "shouted" the trip. <i>(Jun 11, 1964,NZ Observer,4</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

[NOTES: noun.]

>  Last week's story about the canny Otahuhu farmer who managed a seven-shilling "shout" with a five-shilling bottle of whisky is capped by another. <i>(Jun 11, 1904,NZ Observer,16</i>)

>  Often the same group of mates would meet every week, each taking his turn to 'shout' a round of drinks for the group. <i>(Jun 2004,NZ Memories,No. 48/6</i>)

>  He would swear he saw two shouts. <i>(Dec 1, 1917,NZ Truth,2</i>)

>  Before banks had been established, the diggers frequently paid for shouts, meals and beds by doling out gold dust with a teaspoon from a chamois leather bag. <i>(Mar 11, 1924,Otago Witness,60</i>)

>  The fortunate one celebrated the event by a comprehensive "shout". <i>(Jul 16, 1885,Wairarapa Daily,2</i>)

>  He returned the shout, paying only for some ginger ale, which he had in his own whisky. <i>(May 16, 1934,NZ Truth,15</i>)

>  <b>TRIPP</b>  <i>(1863,Lecture on NZ</i>) [NOTES: [check: may be v.: ? sense: see KNOCK DOWN] 1863 Tripp Lecture in 1967 Harper Kettle on Fuchsia 49]

>  <b>LAPHAM</b> There were two of three more shouts. <i>(1880,We Four,25</i>)

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> <i>Shout.</i> `A call to a waiter to replenish the glasses of a company: hence, a turn in paying for a round of drinks. Also, a free drink given to all present by one of the company; a drinking party,' this last being rare: Australian, hence New Zealand; by 1903 (indeed, long before that: see H., 3rd ed., 1864), fairly gen.: 1863, H. Simcox, `Many a `shout' they're treated to.' O.E.D. and Morris. Ex<i> shout</i>, v.i. - 2. Hence, one's turn to entertain another: from ca1885. E.g. `It's my shout this time.' Baumann. <i>(1937,Dictionary of Slang,764</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. drink or round of drinks given to a person or group

[NOTES: noun.]

>  Half-a-dozen luggers, / Waiting for a shout. <i>(May 12, 1906,NZ Truth,47/1/8</i>)

<i>noun</i>. esp. a round of drinks in a school

### shouter

 
<i>noun</i>.

When the shouter has retired I place it back in the box. <i>(Oct 6, 1900,New Zealand Free Lance,10</i>)

### shouting

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  She like himself, is married, and like himself is not allowing the fact to be obtrusive. Now just fancy two "shrewdies" listening to the merry story of the rippling waves, and then to meet with reverses. It is a scream to all. <i>(Dec 23, 1915,Grey River Argus,2</i>)

>  <b>TURNER</b> Established diminutives are ...<i> possie </i> (position or place), ...<i> jelly </i> (gelignite),<i> trammie </i> (tramway worker), ... and <i>shrewdie </i> (a shrewd person). <i>(1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,118</i>)

>  <b>LAURIDSEN</b> At a concert held ... in 1939 one of the local lads came to light with the following limerick: `Certain young fellow, Mick Moody./ Thought that he was a shrewdy./ Bred hens with short legs/ Though he'd get more eggs,/ But all they would do was go broody. <i>(1988,Linton 1889-1989 A Centennial History ...,194</i>)

>  <b>SLATTER</b> Fred Allen comes racing out with the ball for the drop-out, puts in a little shrewdy and sprints away upfield in a sensational run. <i>(1970,On the Ball,138</i>) [NOTES: [spg SHREWDY]]

>  This time, they and their publishers decided to work a shrewdie. They took full advantage of the 30 days allowed under the Copyright Act before sending the three copies north. <i>(Sep 15, 1972,Otago Daily Times,4</i>) [NOTES: (Griffiths Collection)]

>  In most clubs the players pair off with their mates - or in some cases the people the shrewdies feel have the best chances of pulling off a killing. . . <i>(Jun 23, 1974,Sunday Times (NZ),20</i>)

>  <b>MORRIESON</b> Fancy an old shrewdie like him getting taken for a ride like that. <i>(1974,Predicament,16,1981</i>)

>  <i>(informal) </i> a shrewd person <i>(1979,Heinemann NZ Dictionary,1008</i>)

>  <i>shrewdie n. NZ & Austral. sl. </i>(also <i>shrewd-head, shrewdy </i>) shrewd or cunning person. <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,709</i>) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 450]]

>  To rush blindly into the high gear would be fatal. They are `shrewdies', some of those people outside the windows. A man must keep his head <i>(Jan 10, 1916,Triad, The,43</i>)

>  <b>MILLER</b> The shrewdies had used up all the hot water <i>(1939,Camps, Tramps and Trenches,11</i>) [NOTES: (1917 Feb 1) 1939 Miller CT and Ts 11]

>  [spg SHREWDY] There was among them he whom they called Shrewdy ... <i>(Mar 10, 1922,Quick March,11</i>)

>  <b>MARSH</b>  <i>(1937,Vintage Murder,123</i>) [NOTES: [see quot HARD CASE]]

>  <b>BALLANTYNE</b> People reckoned Fred was a shrewdie because he did some bookmaking outside his warehouse business, ... <i>(1948,Cunninghams, The,16,1976</i>)

>  <b>BALLANTYNE</b> People reckoned Fred was a shrewdie because he did some bookmaking outside his warehouse business, ... <i>(1948,Cunninghams, The,16,1976</i>)

>  <b>BOOTH</b> Charlie Mills, who prided himself on being a shrewdie, had slipped farther south than the rest of the fleet.... <i>(1964,Footsteps in the Sea,16</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a shrewd trick, a slinter (espec. work, pull, put a shrewdie)

### shuffle-grazing

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a controlled grazing system that combines ad hoc, set stocking, and rotational grazing. [Stock are grazed in a specific paddock for a week when the gate is opened to a next paddock. Once all of the stock are out of the former enclosure, the gate is closed behind them, the pattern being repeated around 3-4 paddocks. ]

>  Waitomo beef finisher Rusty Tipping uses a shuffle-grazing system to achieve maximum weight gains .. In the shuffle-grazing system each mob is allocated four paddocks stocked at 2.2 bulls per hectare. <i>(Oct 15, 1998,NZ Farmer,13</i>)

>  The result is what he calls shuffle-grazing - where the bulls are grazed in blocks within conventional fencing and shuffled from paddock to paddock according to pasture quality. <i>(Jul 29, 2004,Dominion Post,C6</i>)

### sick

 
<i>adjective</i>.

>  Various chemical modes of cleansing have been tried with only partial success, but recently it was accidentally discovered that a current of electricity would almost immediately expel the troublesome impurities, no matter how abundant or how "sick" the mercury had been rendered. ..With the current flowing, the mercury could not be made sick. <i>(Nov 5, 1883,Evening Post,2</i>)

>  This sick mercury also powders away, or as it is termed "flours," so that the floured fluid metal is carried away and lost, leaving fresh surfaces to be attacked by the injurious ingredients in the ore. <i>(Mar 20, 1890,Otago Witness,12</i>)

>  <b>MAY</b> The mercury plates were seldom perfect: the finest gold was lost by flotation while with cemented gold a thin coating of iron oxide (`rusty gold') often prevented amalgamation. The mercury itself became `sick' or `floured'; both sodium and nitric acid were employed to improve its amalgamating qualities. <i>Ibid.</i> 527 FLOURED MERCURY: mercury that has lost its amalgamating properties because of impurities in the ore or the wash. The mercury is then `sick'. <i>(1967,West Coast Gold Rushes,238</i>)



 
<i>adjective</i>.

>  ... those in the `bush sick' area were inspected and a dozen found to have died ... the herbage grown on the so-called sick country.' <i>Ibid.</i> 40 ... periodical changing of the stock from `sick' to what is known to be `healthy' country every few months. <i>(1928,TrNZI,58/39</i>) [NOTES: (Aston)]

>  [caption] Second crop of lambs from ewes confined to sick paddock, Sherry River. <i>(1938,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,20/195A</i>)



 
<i>adjective</i>. NZ colloquial usage follows US and earlier British usage in assigning a main sense of `ill, unwell, ailing' to this word, esp. in the phrase <i>be sick </i>; contrast modern British usage with main sense `vomit'. That is, NZ usage follows OED a. I 1. Suffering from illness of any kind; ill, unwell, ailing. Now chiefly literary and U.S. [9-19c]. rather than 2. Having an inclination to vomit, or being actually in the condition of vomiting [18-20c]. An ambiguous statement, e.g., `I was sick on Thursday' would usually be interpreted in NZ as `I was ill' etc; in Britain probably as `I vomited etc' (Dr. R. Savage); and this can lead to some immediately horrifying images for Englishmen in N.Z., needing quick reshuffling to extract the correct sense: e.g., I was sick in bed last Thursday. Unambiguous statements naturally assign themselves appropriate senses, mainly on aspectual grounds: I was sick twice before breakfast; I have been sick for months. `Ill' is often used in NZ by, e.g. mothers and nurses, as a euphemism for the `vomit' sense: Little Tommy has just been ill all over his shoes. (When used as a verb, sick is always `vomit': N.Coghill and C. Tolkien have an interesting note to l.71 of their edition of Chaucer's <i>The Nun's Priest's Tale </i> (Harrap pp 94-5). l. 71 Repleccioun [overeating] re made hire nevere sick `sick': `ill', not `sick'. The withering away of the old sense of sick is relatively recent, and has not taken place in America; cf also <i>sickbay, sickroom, a sick man,</i> etc. Chaucer knew the word <i>ill, but for him it was a word characteristic of the North and East of England (it was of Scandinavian origin), and he only used it to give an impression of dialect in the talk of John and Aleyn, the Two Cambridge students from the North of England in the Reeve's Tale; for them, in any case, it meant `bad, evil'. Chaucer's word for being sick (in our sense) was <i>spew</i>.'

>  <b>MARSH</b> ... and I must say he did look a bit sick. <i>(1937,Vintage Murder,96</i>)

>  <b>M.E. ALCOCK</b> I list below the words I can think of [as having different meanings in Britain and NZ]: <i>N.Z. English </i> Singlet Vest Sick Sick in England means to vomit.) <i>(Dec 3, 1957,Letter</i>)</i>

### sickle-fibre

>  Shedding is common among hairy sickle-fibres; sometimes all are shed, while occasionally, at the other extreme, all persist, every intermediate condition being found. Many of these fibres are much shorter than any shed hairy sickle-fibres. <i>(Jan 20, 1933,NZ Journal of Agriculture,13</i>)

>  When a name for these intermediates is needed, the term "super-sickle" is used. <i>(Mar 20, 1933,NZ Journal of Agriculture,141</i>)

>  Fibres of this kind that do not grow after birth are called "baby sickle-fibres." <i>(Mar 20, 1933,NZ Journal of Agriculture,144</i>)

>  Other somewhat longer sickle-fibres, it would appear from their length, are shed after growing for just a short time after birth. These are termed "infant sickle-fibres" (Fig 4). Infant sickle-fibres are much less abundant than baby ones. Most sickle-fibres with coarse medulla in the post-natal region sustain this up to some eight weeks after birth. For these it is convenient to use the term "chalky sickle-fibres," from their dull white appearance. Super-sickle-fibres, some with a good deal of medulla in the neck, occasionally remain fine after birth ... <i>(Mar 20, 1933,NZ Journal of Agriculture,145</i>)

>  The stoutest of birthcoat fibres, halo-hairs, are almost all shed and the super-sickle-fibres with necks coarser than those of sickle-fibres, shed the more readily. <i>(Jun 20, 1934,NZ Journal of Agriculture,342</i>)

### sidle

 
<i>noun</i>. an act of sidling; a track that runs at an angle across a slope.

[NOTES: ca1953 R. Mason e.g. make a high sidle to avoid the bluffs, or a broken ridge.]

>  <b>PASCOE</b> When the Whitcombe River is in flood there are many such whirlpools which the usual route avoids by a high steep sidle in the thick bush. <i>(1960,Over the Whitcombe Pass,33fn</i>) [NOTES: 1863 Lauper in 1960 Pascoe (ed) Over the Whitcombe Pass 33 fn]

>  <b>LAUPER</b> [Note]. There are many such whirlpools which the usual route avoids by a high steep sidle in the thick bush. <i>(1863,Over the Whitcombe Pass</i>) [NOTES: The footnote is a 1960 one by Pascoe.]

>  Near the head of the creek, the track climbs over a saddle of regenerating forest to begin a sidle towards Kaitoke... <i>(2008,NZ Geographic,94/30</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [mustering] to traverse a steep slope [ in a horizontal team formation.]

>  <b>STRONACH</b> Most of the Clarence block is sidled. That is to say, the spurs are so big that it is necessary to have several men sidling on the 'face' or side of each spur. I have seen as many as ten men on a face sidling along about half a mile apart. <i>(1953,Musterer on Molesworth,23</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to negotiable a steep slope of a hill by going round the side of it rather than straight up to the crest. (probably a back form from SIDELING.)

>  To <i>sidle </i>, to go around the side or across the face of a hill, is a characteristic New Zealand expression, strange to the Englishman or Australian. The example of 1821 in O.E.D.: `Ye know the footpath sidles down the hill', suggests that something of the New Zealand meaning was not unknown in England, but it cannot have been well known, or mountaineers would not have started to use <i>traverse </i>, both as a noun and as a verb, towards the end of last century. <i>Sidle </i> is well known among high-country musterers. As it is a word most likely to be used in open hilly or mountainous country, one may guess that musterers and up-country people gave it currency, whence it was adopted by mountain club people. If ski-ing had not brought its more or less international vocabulary with it we should no doubt be sidling slopes, on skis, that we now traverse... From 1936 to 1938 in <i>The Tramper </i> there are a number of references to `sidling tracks' and `sidling routes'. Towards the end of 1938 comes `after sidling round the head of the said stream', and, a year later, `we sidle the top of Three Johns', and from then on the verb flourishes. In 1940 comes `on a long sidle', and from then on the noun is as common as the verb. <i>Ibid.</i> 41 From the top basin we sidled up tiresome scree, ... and at last emerged on the top of the divide. <i>(Sep 1958,Tararua,29</i>) [NOTES: Ruth Mason `Track and Trail']

>  Often, with back bent low, he must thread [sic] the dirty overgrown bed of a steep little watercourse, or, still with back bent, sidle along the muddy slope of a steep hill, through a tunnel in the koromiko copse; or, straightening his back with a sigh of relief as he emerges on the open shingle-bed, find that he has to ford and ford again and again the cold rapid stream, slipping ahd splashing over weed-covered stones. <i>(Aug 18, 1862,Daily Southern Cross,3</i>)

>  A few blows with the tomahawk, a fire-stick judiciously employed, and, should the brook be high, a little sidling over a low bank or two, is the most that can be needed, though the gorge being very narrow, its aspect may at first appear discouraging for a mile or two. <i>(Jun 2, 1855,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2</i>)

>  We sidled along the spurs, slipping and stumbling over the steep, wet, frozen, stony ground, for three of four miles, which seemed interminable, there the river Mataura approaches the hills, and made our course more westerly; a little further on we crossed the Otamita, a mountain stream, that came rushing out from between the hills, with a clear stony bottom. <i>(Oct 3, 1894,North Otago Times,1</i>)

>  Come and let us sidle up thes bonnie brae and ha'e a look roond. <i>(Sep 6, 1905,Otago Witness,86</i>)

>  Come and let us sidle up this bonnie brae and ha'e a look roond. <i>(Sep 6, 1905,Otago Witness,86</i>)

>  <b>BLAIR</b> There was heavy snow as we sidled along above Bealey gully. ... and carelessly sticking to the ridge I carelessly continued sidling. <i>(1956,Life & Work at Canterbury Agricultural College,83</i>) [NOTES: (1926 Hilgendorf in) 1956 Blair Life and Work at Canterbury Agricultural College 83]

>  To work one's way round, up or down a facing by an easy grade. Usually sidle out, sidle round etc. <i>(1933,Press, The</i>) [NOTES: Acland]

>  <b>JONES</b> .... sheer precipice for thousands of feet. One could not sidle round in mustering, but had to go under or over the top. <i>(1933,Autobiography,82</i>)

>  <i>Sidle </i>.-To work one's way round, up, or down a facing by an easy grade. Usually <i>s. out, s. round,</i> etc <i>(Jan 27, 1934,Press, The,15</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> Sidling to a handy shoulder, he scanned the basin ahead. <i>(1949,High Alps of NZ,30</i>)

>   <i>(Oct 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,295/1</i>)

>  <b>R. MASON</b> `To go around the side of; to go along a hill-side. (tramping.) To sidle a hill; to sidle along a valley (not on the ridge, not on the valley floor, but along the hillside.) The man on the top beat, in all but exceptional circumstances, keeps a little in front, and each man down the face is a little behind the man above. <i>(1953,Musterer on Molesworth,23</i>)

>  <b>SUTHERLAND</b> The ceiling of mist was above us when we gained the range beyond the razorback and sidled to a saddle we could see a mile to the south. <i>(1953,Golden Bush, The,168,1963</i>)

<i>noun</i>.

### sidling

 
<i>adjective</i>. .

[NOTES: aka sideling]

>  From 1936 to 1938 in <i>The Tramper </i> there are a number of references to `sidling tracks' and `sidling routes'. Towards the end of 1938 comes `after sidling round the head of the said stream', and, a year later, `we sidle the top of Three Johns', and from then on the verb flourishes. In 1940 comes `on a long sidle', and from then on the noun is as common as the verb. <i>(Sep 1958,Tararua,29</i>) [NOTES: Ruth Mason `Track and Trail']

>  For most of the distance a sideling path six feet wide, has been cut - a good portion of it having been formed through rock - while a ford hitherto used, but very dangerous, in the Waipunga River, has been avoided. <i>(Apr 10, 1858,Hawke's Bay Herald,5</i>)

>  Several have sunk shafts, but having too much water to contend with they have commenced to drive a tunnel from the bottom of the shaft in order to get at the sideling reef, one shaft being 40 feet deep and 40 feet tunnel in length. <i>(Dec 11, 1888,Marlborough Express,3</i>)

>  Mr. Stubbs and one of his sons joined us here, and the four of us shouldered our swags, took a sideling route up the face of the hill on to the Ashley Gorge Saddle ... <i>(Oct 5, 1895,Oxford Observer,3</i>)

>  <b>ROSS</b> At every `spell ho!' the outlook from our sideling bush was lovely. <i>(1889,Complete Guide to Lakes of C.Otago, A,43</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a steep face, gully side or hill cutting around which stock, shepherd or musterer must sidle.

[NOTES: aka sideling]

>  <b>SUTHERLAND</b> A dozen times as we swung down thesidling to the flat below the lake Iwondered whether I had been wise inletting the biggest head I had everlooked at over a rifle go free. <i>(1953,Golden Bush, The,00</i>)

>  They [sc. musterers] can stand days of shingle sidling.. and be quizzicalthrough it all. <i>(Apr 1945,NZ Geographer,I/27</i>)

>  <b>HOLLOWAY</b> June 11th: the whole of the terraces and sidlings are gold-bearing <i>(1874,Journal of a Visit,103</i>)

>  <b>BELL</b> Roads, as the term is generally understood, were for a time unknown. At first, a pathway through the bush or along the felled road line, diving ... into a deep gulley, or skirting a slippery sideling, and barely passable for a horse; then a formed clay track, ... <i>(1899,In the Shadow of the Bush,1</i>)

>  <b>ELWELL</b> He gave up the attempt of climbing the ridge, and made away back along the sidling to my own run again <i>(1878,Boy Colonists,197</i>)

>  <b>WARDON</b> The giant pine tree went crashing down the precipitous sidling into the bottom of the gully. <i>(1892,MacPherson's Gully,11</i>)

>  <b>McKEE WRIGHT</b> I sigh for the good old days in the station whare again; / . The speargrass and cabbage-trees yonder ... / The dark of the bush on the sidlings, ... / <i>(1897,Station Ballads,56</i>) [NOTES: 1897 McKee Wright Station Ballads (`An Old Colonist's Reverie') in Centennial Treasury of Otago Verse 56]

>  <b>BATHGATE</b> Then when we reached the hills we passed along many a sloping piece of ground, called a sidling, with the coach tilted at an angle that seemed to invite an upset. <i>(1925,Random Recollections,25</i>)

>  <i>Face and sidling.-S.</i> is generally used in connection with mustering and connotes the idea of steepness or roughness, and is never used when discussing the aspect. You do not say `a dark <i> s.,' though you often hear `dark side'; but <i>f. can be used in either sense. <i>(Jan 20, 1934,Press, The</i>) [NOTES: contrast FACE]

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> It was only a small cutting at first, but later a long sidling was made on the same ridge and was also called Sailors' Cutting ... <i>(1939,First White Boy Born in Otago,134</i>)

>  <b>SUTHERLAND</b> Directly ahead lay several miles of snow-grass sidling falling from a long ridge flanking its southern side. <i>(1953,Golden Bush, The,167,1963</i>)

>  The river forced us to do much sidling through the tauhinau and matagouri and across a limestone face ... <i>(Sep 1958,Tararua,76</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> <i>Sidling:</i> The face of a hill, i.e. hillside. A man sidles round the face of a hill. <i>(1966,Boss's Story, The,189</i>)

>  <b>BAYLISS</b> Along the steep sideling <i>(1866,Glimpse of Shepherd Life, A,621</i>)

>  <b>BARRINGTON</b> Continued on our course up the river - a very bushy sideling of a steep mountain gorge, with the white foam of the river some hundreds of feet below us - ... <i>(Apr 30, 1864,Diary</i>) [NOTES: 1864 Apr 30 Barrington Diary in 1959 Taylor Early Travellers 409]

>  [We] made a sideling under the top to cross a valley and then go down on a lower ridge. <i>(Oct 10, 1864,Chudleigh Diary,148,1950</i>)

>  ... a most romantic ride through bush over low passes along lovely sidelings looking down into endless valeys [sic] full of dense bush. <i>(Jul 12, 1865,Chudleigh Diary,193,1950</i>)

>  <i>sideling n. NZ </i> (also <i>sidling </i>) steep but negotiable slope. <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,711</i>) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

>  <b>NEWTON</b> <i>Sidling run </i>: A run directly round through the face of a hill, as distinct from running either uphill or down. <i>(1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,169</i>)

>  <b>MUNDY</b> Braed Austr. 1886 w. Som. wordbook; EDD 3. Slope of a hill: sloping ground sCy. I.W. Scun. Austr. <i>(1881,Our Antipodes</i>) [NOTES: 1880 Sc. Jam. 1852 Mundy Our Antipodes 1881]

>  <b>SHORTLAND</b> While passing in front of a hut [at the whaling station], I was invited to visit a sailor who lived within, and who had had a bad leg for many years, which rendered him unfit for any other work than that of signal man. While the rest of his companions were actively engaged in the boats, he was carried every day during the season to the summit of the most projecting point of the cliff, where he sat under a shed, glass in hand, to look out for whales. By means of a mast and yard, and some signals, he was able to give notice to the boats in whatever direction he discovered a whale; and so earned a small share in the fortunes of the fishery. <i>(1851,Southern Districts of NZ,129</i>)

>  Quote 	That clear-felling.. of potentially some 17,000 hectares of virgin native forest covered by the South Island Landless Natives Act (SILNA) is occurring in the 21st century in a country that is marketing itself as "pure" is a tragic short-sighted crime. <i>(Apr 19, 2003,Listener (New Zealand Listener),9</i>)

### silver beech

 
<i>noun</i>. <i>Nothofagus menziesii</i>, often popularly and locally called silver birch, a variety of native beech found mainly in rainy areas.

>  Silver-beech and entire-leaved beech are found as far south as Preservation Inlet and the Tautuku Forest, while the mountain-beech prefers higher levels, ... <i>(1902,Settler's Handbook of NZ, The,120</i>)

### sinking for the Queen

 
<i>phrase</i>. [historical]

>  <b>MAY</b> DUFFER: applied to a rush, a shaft, or a claim generally. A failure. Synonyms were `shicer', `stringer' or, in the case of a false rush, `store-keepers' rush'. A claim which was exhausted was said to be `duffered out'. At Ross in 1866 putting down a duffer shaft was termed `sinking for the Queen'. Duffers (Creek) is a common West Coast place-name. <i>(1962,West Coast Gold Rushes,526</i>) [NOTES: 1967 ed.]

### six o'clock swill

 
<i>noun</i>. a popular name for the 5-6 p.m. drinking rush during the six o'clock closing of bars before 9 October 1967

[NOTES: [AND see SWILL: six o'clock swill 1955]]

>  I also worked in the Great Northern Hotel in the days of the six o'clock swill - everybody was paralytic at six. <i>(Jun 1999,Metro,56</i>)

>  Sir, - Like the great majority of New Zealanders who finish work at 5 or 5.30 p.m. I like two or three beers and a chat to my friends before I go home for dinner. That is when I feel like a drink, and when I enjoy it. They call it the `six o'clock swill,' but we enjoy it. After all, when service is required by so many at the same time, there must be a crush. <i>(Aug 13, 1963,Dominion,4</i>)

>  New Zealander's liquor hours, notably the `five to six swill' produced gusty debate and plenty of laughs at the National Party Conference yesterday. <i>(Jul 23, 1963,Dominion,1</i>)

>  <b>TURNER</b> This gives in New Zealand the terms <i>vertical drinking </i>(in crowded bars with standing room only), <i>the six o'clock swill</i> and, at least among students in Wellington about 1940, the <i>shicker express</i>, the first tram after six o' clock ... <i>(1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,131</i>)

>  The rich linguistic legacy of the election rituals would draw thousands. Coaches would tour vivid re-enactments of the six o'clock swill, staged by Richard Campion and choreographed after extensive interviews with the survivors.[check with MITCHELL cit???] <i>(Jun 25, 1972,Sunday Times (NZ),35/2</i>)

>  <b>MITCHELL</b> Coaches would tour vivid re-enactments of the six o'clock swill ... . <i>(1972,Half-Gallon Quarter-Acre Pavlova Paradise, The,14</i>)

>  <b>GEBBIE & McGREGOR</b> We had knocked off one Thursday night after [47] the six o'clock swill and were having a drink in the upstairs bar about nine o'clock ... <i>(1979,Incredible 8-Ounce Dream,46</i>)

>  <b>LELAND</b> <i>six o'clock swill</i>: Prior to 9 October 1967, bars in New Zealand had to close at 6.00p.m. (now they close at 10.00p.m., often 12.00p.m. ..) on weekends. <i>(1980,Personal Kiwi-Yankee Dictionary, A,92</i>)

>  <i>Wellington</i> New Zealanders will choose in a referendum later this year between their notorious 6 o'clock swill and a more civilized style of drinking liquor. .. Paradoxically, the appalling conditions of the 5-to-6-o'clock swill have strengthened the opponents of reform. <i>(Jun 29, 1967,San Francisco Chronicle,4</i>) [NOTES: 1967 July 29 Ian Templeton in San Francisco Chronicle 4]

>  <b>HOLCROFT</b> We were then .. in the heyday of the six o'clock swill, an institution so notorious that visiting Americans .. were taken to selected hotels to see for themselves an operation otherwise unbelievable. <i>(1986,Sea of Words,9</i>)

>  <i>six o'clock swill NZ & Austral. colloq.</i> (formerly) period of rapid consumption of alcoholic drinks immediately before six o'clock closing-time of bars. <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,717</i>) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

>  `Privatisation', `Corporatisation' and `market-driven forces' are now as common in our vocabulary as the `six o'clock swill' and `Don Clarke' was to our forebears. <i>(Sep 21, 1987,Salient,5</i>)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>six o'clock swill </i> rapid male drinking in male-only public bars in the lead-up to 6 pm pub closing time, usually from end of work at 5 pm. Perceived as piggish and the closest we got to a direct connection between beer hoses and customers. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,103</i>)

>  Though the six o'clock swill ceased in 1967 .. there was still a powerful linkage between drinking beer and masculinity. <i>(Mar 13, 1988,Dominion Sunday Times,16</i>)

>  We introduced daylight saving time when it suited us, abolished the six o'clock swill and have reshaped the school year into four terms. <i>(Feb 22, 1997,Listener (New Zealand Listener),7</i>)

>  They have become booze barns run by a private company which is still in the six o 'clock swill mode . <i>(Jan 20, 1993,Independent Herald (Wellington),1</i>)

>  Maybe one day we'll look back on Sunday closure with the same amazement with which we now view the six o'clock swill, but surely never with the same horror. <i>(Aug 13, 1990,Listener (New Zealand Listener),15</i>)

>  <b>GOLDSMITH</b> These establishments [sc. illegal beer houses] catered for those who wanted to drink past the '6 o'clock swill'. <i>(1997,John Banks : A Biography,40</i>)

>  <b>Michael King</b> With the abolition of six o'clock closing of hotel bars in 1967 and an eventual relaxation of restaurant licensing laws, alcohol became available at more civilised hours and in more civilised circumstances than in the days of the 'six o'clock swill'. <i>(2003,Penguin History of New Zealand,389</i>)

>  The teen-age binge-drinking so evident at the New Year is part of a New Zealand tradition that goes right back to the six o'clock swill, known affectionately as the six o'clock spill. <i>(Feb 10, 2001,Listener (New Zealand Listener),32</i>)

>  For husbands, release from their emotional repression came only with the "six o'clock swill" at the pub or Saturdays at the footy. <i>(Sep 19, 1987,Listener (New Zealand Listener),31</i>)

>  In the dim glow of yellow lights, you can smell again the perpetually beer-soaked carpets of the  six o'clock swill and consider that you are just another battery hen queueing for a fix. <i>(Apr 8, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),52</i>)

>  When licensing laws were relaxed in 1989, and again in 1999, to allow the sale of alcohol in supermarkets and, it turns out, dairies, the changes were supposed to reflect a new, more mature, attitude to drinking. After weaning a lamb is called a <i>hogget until shorn. A male lamb is a <i>ram lamb</i> until castrated, then a <i>wether</i>. A female lamb is a <i>ewe lamb</i>. After shearing, a ewe or ram lamb is usually called a <i>shorn hogget </i> until cutting the first two teeth. It is then called a <i>two-tooth</i>. Some use the term two-tooth as soon as the lamb is shorn. Next year the sheep is a <i>four-tooth</i>, then a <i>six-tooth</i> and then an <i>eight-tooth </i> or <i>full-mouthed</i> sheep. >  <b>POLACK</b> Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called <i>para</i>[as-acute] </i> paraua</i>[a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, <i>mungu nui</i> (black physeter); right whale, <i>tohora</i> (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, <i>mango</i> (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, limpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. <i>(1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/202fn</i>)

### skillion

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a section of a woolshed where sheep are kept under cover.

>  <b>BUTLER</b> In a woolshed the aisles would be called skilions .. All the sheep go into the skilions. <i>(1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,158</i>)

>  <b>BARKER</b> A constant succession of woolly sheep being brought up to fill the 'skillions' ... <i>(1865,Station Life in NZ,34</i>)

>  He looked into his woolshed and said, 'Oh yes, there's plenty of room in the skillions.' [skilion] <i>(Dec 2, 1933,Press, The  (Acland Glossary),15</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [obsolete] (in pl.)

See: -

>  <b>BUTLER</b> The wool-shed .... has a large central space, and an aisle-like partition on each side. These last will be for holding the sheep at night. ... In a wool-shed, the aisles would be called skilions (whence the name is derived, I know not, nor whether it has two `l's' in it or one). All the sheep go into the skillions <k>Ibid.</i> x/158 In a wool-shed the aisles would be called skilions (whence the word is derived I know not, nor whether it has two l's in it or one). All the sheep go into the skilions. The shearers shear in the centre ... [and] pull the sheep out of the skilions as they want them. <i>(1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,139</i>)

>  <b>BARKER</b> ... a constant succession of woolly sheep being brought up to fill the `skillions' (from whence the shearers take them when they want them), and the newly-shorn ones ... being turned out after they have passed through a narrow passage, called a `race,' where each sheep is branded ... <i>(1865,Station Life in NZ,34,1870</i>)

>  <i>Skillion</i>.- [Variant of 'skillin' and skilling', recorded from the fourteenth century, all late examples being provincial English; origin unknown. --A.W.] In old Australian and New Zealand books (up to about 1880) it is common and means the sheep-holding part of a woolshed. I can remenber an old hand mentioning the word in the 'nineties. I have tried it on several elderly shepherds since the war I and none of them understood it. I imagined the word had gone completely out of use until last month (May 1933), when I bought five tons of chaff from a man and asked him to store it for a few weeks. He looked into his woolshed and said, `Oh yes, there's plenty of room in the skillions.' I felt as if I had met a notornis. ' . . called skillions (whence the name is derived I know not, nor whether it has two l's in it or one). All the sheep go into the skilions.' (Butler A First Year in Canterbury Settlement], p. 139). `A constant succession of woolly sheep being brought up to fill the skillions.' ([1874 Lady Barker Station Life], p. 34). <i>(Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  <b>TEMPLE</b> ... he saw the clearest satisfaction in the sunlight falling through the skillion door over the heaving backs of the sheep and on to the board, slick with wool grease ... <i>(1979,Stations,99</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a lean-to; a built-on room, shed, etc.

[NOTES: also in combinations (skillion roof, kitchen, cottage, etc.)]

>  <b>CHEVALIER</b> A skillion kitchen with a big fire. <i>(1866,Reminiscences of a Journey,23</i>)

>  <b>SALMOND</b> <i>Skillion (roof)</i>. a single-pitch roof or `lean-to' attached to a building to enclose extra rooms; also known as a <i>skilling. </i> <i>(1986,Glossary of Building Terminology,233</i>)

>  As in the case with bush houses, two skillen-rooms would be added behind <i>(1852,Colonial Church Chronicle,6/294</i>)

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> (Mr Busbridge drew me a plan of the place, and its five compartments. One of these, a long room known as the `Skillion' had rows of bunks along each wall. <i>(1947,Pioneer Recollections,21,1956</i>) [NOTES: (sc. on an Otago station)]

>  In a similar way the baled straw can be built to form the walls of a shelter-shed, with a skillion roof made of saplings overlaid with thatch and supported, where necessary, by forked uprights. <i>(Jun 7, 1919,Evening Post,11</i>)

The common name Bonita is not to be confusd with Bonito which is Skipjack Tuna, (<i>Katsuwonus pelamis</i>). <i>Ibid.</i> 49-50 <i>TUNA</i> (3 species excluding Albacore) (a) Scientific name: (i) <i>Katsuwonus pelamis</i> (ii) <i>Thunnus maccoyi</i> (iii)<i> Thunnus albacares.</i> (b) Suggested commercial name[s]: (i) Skipjack Tuna (ii) Southern Bluefin Tuna (iii) Yellowfin Tuna. (c) Other common names: (i) Skipjack; Striped Bonito (ii) Bluefin Tuna; Southern Bluefin; Southern Tuna (iii) Yellowfin All sometimes referred to as Tunny. (d) Principal localities where taken: (i) A summewr visitor to New Zealand ... (ii) Southern Bluefin Tuna is a large species of temperate Australasian seas and migrates south to Foveaux Strait in summer months. ### sky the towel

 
<i>phrase</i>. to die

>  Mafish.- Sam Slang remarks; It is well known how the Turkish word `mafish' is commonly used now in place of old slang, such as `gone a million,' `blown out,' `snuffed it,' `clenched his fist,' `crashed in,' `handed in his checks,' `took the count,' `skied the towel,' etc. <i>(Nov 1, 1918,Quick March,15</i>)

>  GONE WEST. [headline] Mr. A.H. Logan. On Wednesday night last [13 August 1931] ... Logan sailed to that mystic land beyond the setting sun to await - The Morn!
