### skyshaft

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>McARA</b> <i>Overwind</i>: Failure by the engine-driver to stop his machine before the safety detaching-hook on the winding-rope came into contact with the detaching ring mounted in the headframe, thus suspending the cage in the skyshaft and allowing the rope to go over the head-sheave pulley. Overwinds had to be reported to the Inspector of Mines. To prevent overwind there were generally two warning bells which rang in the engine-room as the cage was approaching the surface. <i>(1978,Gold Mining at Waihi (Glossary),328</i>)

### slab

 
<i>noun</i>. a fish in poor condition (?)

>  Another important [trout] food was a small mollusc ... of which no less than 140 were counted in the stomach of a `slab' taken at Rotorua. ... A considerable number of the trout examined were definitely `slabs'. The slabby condition appeared to be due not only to the usual poor health of the fish for some months after spawning had taken place, but more definitely to both semi-starvation and indigestion. <i>(1921,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,3/272</i>) [NOTES: (Tillyard)]

>  <b>HINTZ</b> Anglers complain about the presence of `slabs'; the marine biologists sustain their complaints by proving that the lake holds `an undue proportion of matured trout'. <i>Ibid.</i> 171 And if you land your fish you are well rewarded. The kelts and slabs seem to have little chance of competing with vigorous, well-conditioned trout during a green beetle rise. <i>(1964,Trout at Taupo,67</i>)

>  <b>ANDERSON</b> It was a rainbow and it was a `slab'. I don't know what was wrong with it but its body was just bones and not very much longer than its big head. <i>(1957,Men of the Milford Road,197</i>) [NOTES: (Griffiths Collection)]

>  Another important [trout] food was a small mollusc ... of which no less than 140 were counted in the stomach of a `slab' taken at Rotorua. ... A considerable number of the trout examined were definitely `slabs'. The slabby condition appeared to be due not only to the usual poor health of the fish for some months after spawning had taken place, but more definitely to both semi-starvation and indigestion. <i>(1921,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,3/272</i>) [NOTES: (Tillyard)]

>  But of course lots of the fish are "slabs" that should be returned because they are not the best eating. <i>(Dec 2, 2005,NZ Herald,Super Sport D15</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a pack of (12 or 24) beer cans

>  In a dark corner.. about 10 youths two patched Black Power members in their twenties are drinking a slab of beer, whisky and on assortment of other spirits. <i>(Jun 4, 1999,Dominion,11</i>)

>  Does this mean he is one of "them" or can I proceed with my plans for next Friday night's seduction - a slab of beer (on me) and the latest Oasis CD at full volume? <i>(Sep 29, 1997,Dominion,12</i>)

>  I couldn't drink a slab without falling over. <i>(Jul 29, 1999,Listener (New Zealand Listener),64</i>) [NOTES: if not 64, try 43]

>  <b>HUGHES</b> Only the driver had drunk less than a slab of Stein-grenades in the course of the eleven-hour journey. <i>(1999,Shooting from the Lip,158</i>)

>  A couple of country jokers take their Auckland cuz fishing, then send him off to the nearest pub for a slab. <i>(May 14, 1994,Listener (New Zealand Listener),33</i>)

>  An average fishing day for him is a "six-pack day" with a really bad day being "a slab". <i>(Nov 8, 2000,Independent Business Weekly,21</i>)

>  Throw a sheila in the front and the dogs in the back, there's only really room in the boot for a box of .308 shells and a slab of Speights. <i>(Dec 12, 2001,Evening Post Drive,3</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to support (sides of a shaft, well, etc) with slabs [AND mining 1854]; (also vbl n slabbing

>  The road from Kapanga to Ring's diggings is nearly impassable.  It is slabbed two-thirds of the way by Messrs Ring, and the government might easily have the remaining portion slabbed and made fit for bullock drays. <i>(Jul 8, 1862,Daily Southern Cross,3</i>)

>  This shaft is sunk to a depth of 30 feet, the whole distance being slabbed through blue sediment. <i>(Oct 6, 1893,West Coast Times,2</i>)

>  Before stating anything farther, it may be necessary to say that there were three branches of gold-digging we did not try, viz. - turning the water in creeks or streams of any size, to try the beds of them, because we were not strong enough, and on account of the time it would take; sinking in flats, where the holes might go deep and require to be slabbed ... <i>(Jun 20, 1857,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2</i>)

>  No 2. shaft is sunk to a depth of 41 feet as follows:- 21 feet slabbed at 4s per ft., - GBP4 4s; 20 feet not slabbed at 3s per ft., - GBP3; 3 feet additional, No 1. shaft, at 3s, 9s.  total GBP7 13s. <i>(Oct 6, 1893,West Coast Times,2</i>)

>  Sinking on the head lead of the south-west extension 30ft or 40ft, all slabbed, and a quarter of a mile wide, but the washdirt is in patches. <i>(Oct 11, 1876,Tuapeka Times,2</i>)

>  ... the slabbing in a mine <i>(1865,Evening Post,1/245/2</i>)

>  <b>LADY BARKER</b> Wood was wanted for building a stockyard, or slabbing a well <i>(1873,Station Amusements in NZ,3</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> mining term: to keep up the sides of a shaft with timber slabs. [1871] <i>(1898,Austral English,420</i>)

>  <i> slab n.</i> coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. <i> slab v.</i> to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs.<i> slab n. </i> a horse in poor condition. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625</i>)

>  <i> slab n.</i> coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. <i> slab v.</i> to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs.<i> slab n. </i> a horse in poor condition. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18</i>)

>  <b>MAY</b> Drives, too scantily lathed, collapsed; shafts, too hastily slabbed, caved-in; <i>(1967,West Coast Gold Rushes,280,1962</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a rough plank split from a log (perhaps still holding the general sense of slab ); often split slab of wood;  outside cuts, or rough offcuts, of logs (in early days, often used for rough constructions, hence slab-house, slab-hut).

>  <b>CHAPMAN</b> Sometimes the whare is built of large "Slabs"; sometimes of toi-toi (a sort of bulrush), sometimes of wattled clay; and sometimes of brushwood. <i>(1847,Letters to His Father, 1843-1851,00</i>) [NOTES: Quoted in Miller; Early Victorian NZ, p. 140]

>  The old-time navvies' camps on the Main Trunk Railway were rough ephemeral affairs of slab and canvas. <i>(May 2, 1928,NZ Free Lance,7</i>)

>  <b>McRAE</b> The house itself was large - fourteen rooms - and made of plastered slab. <i>(1963,By the Braes of Balquether,31</i>)

>  Also, the house adjoining the brickyard, being a two-roomed slab building, with brick chimney, wooden partition, floored, and having two casements and two doors; ... <i>(Apr 29, 1843,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,237</i>)

>  The new tenants of the land have made improvements in clearing, fencing and erecting houses, most of them being composed of nikau and slabs. <i>(Dec 17, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,8</i>)

>  <b>BRIGHT</b> The walls were formed of broad upright slabs of timber. <i>(1841,Handbook for Emigrants,22</i>)

>  The partitions which are very rough (made of slabs, the outside board in sawing up a tree, bark on one side) do not reach up to the roof. <i>(Apr 20, 1851,Richmond-Atkinson Papers,1/94</i>) [NOTES: (H.R. Richmond)]

>  John & Seal cutting firewood Jem & Georgie splitting slabs for pig-stye <i>(May 1, 1856,Journal Kept at Rockwood and the Point</i>) [NOTES: 1856 May 1 Phillips Rockwood Journal [ATB FS TS 31/Cant.Pub. Lib. 37]]

>  <b>PAUL</b> You are fairly entitled to something better than a warre[e-acute], say a two-roomed hut for yourself ... and a large, strong wata, or store raised on posts to keep your provisions safe from rats. ... slabs plastered with clay are also used for walls ... One of these huts must serve you for your first year's wool-shed, with the help of a few hurdles in front, ... <i>(1857,Letters from Canterbury, NZ,90</i>)

>  <b>HODDER</b> ... slabs of which the tenement was made. <i>(1862,Memories of NZ Life,155</i>)

>  We are now busy putting up a sheep yard we are making of upright slabs with a cross rail and rammed in the ground. <i>(1861,McLean Papers,20/70</i>) [NOTES: (Condie, Hawkesburn Station Canterbury)]

>  <b>WHITWORTH</b> The hut was made of slabs ... [rough cut trunks] <i>(1875,Cobb's Box,6</i>)

>  <b>BULLER</b> At nearly every bend, a rude and lonely hut was standing. This was made of slabs, and thatched with grass. <i>(1878,Forty Years in NZ,27</i>)

>  <b>FEATON</b> To strengthen their defences two detachments ... were detailed to cut slabs in the bush. <i>(1879,Waikato War,52</i>)

>  <b>PRINCE</b> The Beech Hut is built of slabs with a tree-fern roof, and contains eight sleeping berths ... <i>(1889,Diary of a Trip,10</i>)

>  <b>ARTHUR</b> ... Covered at the bottom with wire-netting or `slabs' (split pieces of wood) <i>(1894,Kangaroo and Kauri,98</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> <i> slab n.</i> coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. <i> slab v.</i> to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs.<i> slab n. </i> a horse in poor condition. <i> Slab, n.</i> In English, the word <i> slab </i>, as applied to timber, means `an outside piece taken from a log in sawing it into boards, planks, etc.' (`Webster.') In Australia, the word is very common, and denotes a piece of timber, two or three inches thick: a coarse plank, axe-hewn, not sawn. Used for the walls of rough houses. <i>(1898,Austral English,420</i>)

>  <b>BAUCKE</b> It is a low whare of split slabs, adzed over, and sunk into the earth as closely as the inequalities of adze-joining will permit. <i>(1905,Where the White Man Treads,259</i>)

>  <b>MACDONALD</b> ... then I split slabs and made all the furniture I considered necessary. <i>(1910,Reminiscences,33</i>)

>  Our new home of two rooms with timber hewn out of trees and split into lengths called `slabs' and put up in the rough state. <i>(1916,Letter</i>) [NOTES: 1916 Letter in 1939 Winter The King Country 13]

>  <b>MILLER</b> Sometimes the whare is built of large `Slabs';[sic cap] sometimes of toi-toi (a sort of bulrush), sometimes of wattled clay; and sometimes of brushwood. <i>(1958,Early Victorian NZ,140</i>)

>  A flat thick piece of material; it may be stone or even cake. In Australia and New Zealand a slab is a thick plank; a `slab-hut' is a shanty built of such planks. <i>(1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),370</i>)

>  <i> slab n.</i> coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. <i> slab v.</i> to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs.<i> slab n. </i> a horse in poor condition. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625</i>)

>  <i> slab n.</i> coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. <i> slab v.</i> to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs.<i> slab n. </i> a horse in poor condition. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18</i>)

>  Your chimney must be built of slabs. <i>(Jul 1863,Southern Monthly Magazine,1(5) : 21</i>)

>  The kauta or cooking houses, are proportionably large;  in that part of the pah belonging especially to Heuheu, there is a row of cooking houses 40 feet long by fifteen broad, and 10 feet high in the walls;  which are constructed of enormous slabs, well fitted together;  round windows, with sliding shutters, admit the light, and let out the smoke. <i>(Mar 19, 1842,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3</i>)

>  The hut is of split slabs with a good roof of thatch to defy the weather. <i>(Mar 6, 1890,Otago Witness,40</i>)

>  <b>BIRD</b> The slabs (waste wood) and flitches fall on to mechanically driven rollers controlled by the off-bearer. <i>(1998,Viaducts against the Sky,38</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. often with bark still adhering, trimmed by saw from a log or baulk of timber

### slagged

 
<i>adjective</i>. [Rural] [of land or feed] topdressed with slag.

>  The most notable feature of these tests, which extended over nine grazing seasons, including that of 1906, was the remarkable live weight increase furnished by the slagged portions of the field. <i>(May 27, 1908,Otago Witness,7</i>)

>  The carrying-capacity of the untreated Cockle Park land for the twenty weeks' grazing season was 2 sheep to the acre, which was increased to 4 sheep on the slagged and 2.7 on the superphosphate-dressed plots. Mr G L Marshall .. estimated the carrying-capacity of the slagged paddock as 5.23 sheep. <i>(Jan 20, 1919,NZ Journal of Agriculture,16</i>)

>  The relative merits of superphosphate and basic slag for pasture top-dressing are much discussed in certain districts, particularly North Taranaki and North Auckland. Many experienced farmers are firmly of the opinion that slagged pastures have better milk production and fattening capacities than ones treated with superphosphate. How much this may be due to a greater effect from slag, how much to some effect on the mineral content of the herbage, and how much due to management it is impossible to say. <i>(1936,Agricultural Organization in NZ,389</i>)

>  This season the slagged plot was so much improved that it has carried twelve sheep for four months, whereas the untreated plot is much barer with only six sheep. <i>(Jan 28, 1899,Southland Times,6</i>)

>  In some trials made at Cockle Park Agricultural Station the "slagged" soil, which had been longest under treatment, produced - as compared with "unslagged" soil - about 140 per cent. more oats, 30 per cent. more mustard (first crop), 70 per cent. more mustard (second crop), and about 40 per cent. more wheat, the average increase at Cockle Park being 62 per cent. <i>(Mar 17, 1917,Evening Post,10</i>)

>  Every agriculturist knows that it is not customary to place stock on land immediately it has been slagged, but it may be done when the dew has carried the phosphate into the land or immediately after a fall of rain. <i>(Nov 5, 1921,Evening Post,16</i>)

### slash

 
<i>noun</i>. forestry thinnings; the accumulation of useless material such as prunings, loppings, first thinnings etc `slashed' from trees as part of their silviculture or felling, and left lying on the ground

[NOTES: ca1940 at least; NZ Forest Service]



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] vegetative debris, cut scrub or branches, ready for burning.

>  <b>SALISBURY</b> We had successfully carried out a controlled burn on the slash and stumps some six weeks before the carpenters arrived to erect the woolshed. <i>(1994,I Was So Lucky,259</i>)

### slash and burn

 
<i>phrase</i>. [Rural] [used elsewhere, but sign. in N.Z.history of pastoral land development] the cutting and burning of native flora.

>  For around a century, pasture management was often reminiscent of the primitive 'slash and burn' practised by shifting agriculturists. <i>(Aug 2002,Forest & Bird,25</i>)

### slather

 
<i>verb</i>. box, fight, do battle

See: slather n.

>  On the 28th of this month, Gisborne stoush lovers will have another bonzer night, when the Gisborne Association will bring Bert Lowe and Bill Bartlett together. These two are scheduled to slather for fifteen rounds, but this is not going to be nearly all the fun. Viv Lowe and Poesy will try to deal out oblivion to each other during six rounds, while Mellow and Heany and also Harrison and Frurie will put up their 'dukes'. <i>(May 23, 1914,NZ Truth,6</i>)

>  <b>ANTHONY</b> They [sc. hungry cows] slathered at the mouth, with hunger and eagerness .. <i>(1927,Gus Tomlins,91,1977 ed. Sturm</i>) [NOTES: (?is this an authorial error)]



 
<i>noun</i>. vigorous 'unscientific' fighting; unrestrained toe-to-toe boxing action

[NOTES: from the idea of slathering or plastering blows on one's opponent (often in the collocation 'slather and whack'); see OED slather sense 3 to thrash, defeat thoroughly; see also open slather; compare slather-up n.]

>  [In the last round they both tired visibly, and casting caution to the winds slathered each other.] ... A wild slather ended when Finnie missed with a left and came in with his head low, owing to the impetus. ... Early in the round, Bennetts emerged from a slather, shaking his head and seemed to forget all about his opponent. <i>(Aug 1, 1914,NZ Truth,12</i>)

>  Then both warriors made a speech, which was lost amid the roar. It was a great slather and whack fight. There is no gainsaying Grim's pluck and ability to take punishment. But there is a big chunk of his reputation gone now that Griffin dropped him. <i>(Dec 12, 1908,NZ Truth,3</i>)

>  Chris. Rusterholz (8.5) versus Cliff Pearce (7.12). This was the tit-bit of the evening and provided five rounds of ding dong slather of a high order. Both are quick two-handed fighters and they went at it hammer and tacks without a dull moment intervening. <i>(Mar 4, 1922,NZ Truth,8</i>)

>  The feathers, J. Whittome (8.7) and C. McCarthy (8.5), followed, and they gave a clean, clever exhibition, more like a professional bout than that of amateurs. There was none of that wild slather, but good, scientific punching throughout. <i>(Dec 24, 1921,NZ Truth,8</i>)

>  Seldom indeed has a crowd voiced its approval of an out-and-out boxing match as it did at Wellington last week. Scientific stuff nine times out of ten leaves the audience cold - it is the slather and whack artists that get 'em on their feet, yelling encouragement. But the exception was bumped into last week when Jack Carroll gained a points decision over Charlie Purdy. Carroll came to us with a reputation of a bit of a killer, but his first fight in Wellington showed he was more of a stylist. He showed up as a nice mover, possessing plenty of speed at both ends, but totally lacking as a purveyor of hefty wallops. <i>(Aug 16, 1928,NZ Truth,10</i>)

>  BOXING AT GREYMOUTH. ...Now, when the time is ripe, it might be mentioned that Cook's exhibition throughout the mill, his genuine smile of good fellowship when picking up his opponent on a couple of occasions when he slipped, and his palpable desire to box instead of indulging in 'slather and whack', bears the impression that when his recent mill with Billy Hannan at Gisborne was declared 'no fight' and he lost his share of the purse, there was some truth in his words, 'I don't profess to be a fighter; I'm a boxer, pure and simple, and I tried my hardest to beat Hannan.' <i>(Mar 28, 1914,NZ Truth,6</i>)

### slather up

 
<i>verb</i>. thrash, hammer; castigate; get the better of, defeat (in fighting or words)

[NOTES: variant of OED slather v. sense 3]

>  NORTH AUCKLAND FARMERS CO-OPERATIVE LIMITED. ... Looking at the paid up capital, viz., GBP120,376, and taking a glance at the reserve for income tax (GBP9468) the astounding position is discovered that the preference shareholders are practically receiving fifteen per cent., and for that reason the ordinaries are only able to get a seven per cent. dividend, and they, too, are "slathered up" for eight per cent. of taxation. <i>(Nov 23, 1918,NZ Truth,4</i>)

>  I read a lot of chucks off [sic] about our Member in your paper, but I reckon our Member slathered up the capitalistic class to some tune in his speech the other night. <i>(Dec 15, 1915,Grey River Argus,3</i>)

>  THE CARTERTON SHOOTING TRAGEDY ...Then Spicer came on the scene and drew them aside, and they started to talk about 'slathering up somebody'. ...  Describing what lead [sic] up to the shooting, accused said Rzoska said at the hotel, 'I hear you want to slather me up. I hear you want to have a smack at me!' <i>(Feb 12, 1921,NZ Truth,5</i>)

>  These officers and men, commented upon at the time of their departure as 'the flower of New Zealand's manhood' etc., went to Samoa expecting to slather up the Germans. When they got there they found that the Teuton preferred to leave out the slather, and the eager lads had to enter upon the dull dreary round of garrison life. <i>(Mar 27, 1915,NZ Truth,7</i>) [NOTES: also slather n. here (q.v.)]

>  "That I slathered up a Federationist last night," William Newton Railway Guard sworn said ... <i>(Feb 7, 1913,Ohinemuri Gazette,2</i>)

>  Our visit ended at Nelson - generally spoken of as "Sleepy Hollow." <i>(Sep 24, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,28</i>)

I've heard it said that you'll sleep a couple of hours longer here than you will anywhere else - it's something to do with the air, they say.' <i>(1956,Green Kiwi,172,1960</i>)

>  <b>BATHGATE</b> ... Nelson dubbed `Sleepy Hollow' <i>(1874,Colonial Experiences,275</i>)

>  The `Sleepy Hollow' boys [sc. the Nelson football team] rode rough shod over boisterous Wellington. <i>(1877,Country Journal,1/251</i>)

>  <b>WILSON</b> The air here is positively intoxicating, ... in summer, when the heat is semi-tropical, I am told that Nelson fully merits its soporific title of `Sleepy Hollow'. <i>(1894,In the Land of the Tui,218</i>) [NOTES: 1891 Sep 24 in 1894 Wilson Land of the Tui 218]

### slew

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] an angle left or right that sheep take when they are responding to a dog's direction to change course.

>  Went clean through first flags without trouble and put in a good clean slew, which landed his sheep across the creek. Made a poor slew at the first flags ... <i>(Sep 1, 1925,NZ Farmer,1343</i>)

>  Slew - the angles - left or right - of a hunt and the new direction sheep take when directed to by a dog. <i>(Dec 15, 1983,NZ Journal of Agriculture,45</i>)

>  <b>GORDON</b> By this time, the sheep would be finishing the first set and a right-hand slew had to be applied to line them up for the second set. <i>(1998,Three Sheep and a Dog,151</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [shepherding] to direct sheep in a particular direction.

>  This dog's sheep drifted through first flags, with the dog not interested, but he slewed nicely and he crossed the creek with firm work. <i>(Sep 1, 1925,NZ Farmer,1343</i>)

>  if the driving was done by a huntaway dog, slewing the sheep would be in order. <i>(May 1933,NZ Farmer,317</i>)

>  <b>ACLAND</b> .. if you slewed a mob of strong merino wethers too hard against a fence, the fence went flat. <i>(1946,Early Canterbury Runs,40</i>)

>  <b>HARTLEY</b> The next lesson is devised to teach a dog in advance how to slew sheep. <i>(1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,17</i>)

>  The 'Lake' country is mainly open shingle and it's mostly 'topside' work - slewing sheep downhill. <i>(Apr 11, 1968,NZ Farmer,45</i>)

>  <b>MCLEOD</b> Wait would head or hunt or slew with uncanny intelligence. <i>(1970,Many a Glorious Morning,142</i>)

>  <b>KERR</b> Otairi's huntaways were used to lifting sheep; mine to slewing from above. <i>(2000,High Times in the High Country,173</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to beat, outwit, baffle

[NOTES: SOED labels Aust. & NZ]

>  <b>PYKE</b> Of their reputation, the miners spoke with bated breath; ... The general impression seemed to be, that Jack Ketch had been `slued' (<i>anglice</i> - robbed of his dues) by the trio. <i>(1873,Wild Will Enderby,1/xi/41,(1889,1974)</i>)

>  In London the peelers down areas will go, / To make love to the cook and the victuals, /But here there're no areas down which to intrude, / So of course the New Zealand bobbies are slewed. <i>(1875,NZ Songster,No.3/89</i>) [NOTES: Thatcher London and the Diggings]

>  <b>MITCHELL</b> ... or levant from Oamaru/ Without bidding them adieu/ And the merchants we will slew - let them catch us if they can. <i>(1889,Rhymes and Rambles,25</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  "This Scott seems a nice, steady-going sort of a dog. That was a nice slew he made had it been in the right place." <i>(Jun 3, 1897,Otago Witness,34</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> He [a sheep dog] was so fast that I'd have him away out, past, and beyond any sheep almost before they knew he was coming. In this way I could get in good slews ... <i>Ibid.</i> 169 <i>Slew</i>: To turn or change the direction in which sheep are travelling. To top-side slew is to turn or hunt them downhill. Slewing is done mainly with huntaways and in one of the huntaways events at our trials - Class III - the sheep are hunted on a zig-zag course. This is often called a slew. <i>(1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,26</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>.

>  T. Prendergast's Tom hunted his sheep out well about 300yds and slewed to the right, but failed to slew to the left. <i>(Jun 1, 1893,Otago Witness,21</i>)

>  The dog had to head sheep, slew them, drive them a short distance along a ridge, and then pull to ring. <i>(Apr 15, 1910,Hawera & Normanby Star,7</i>)

>  In class 3 Mr Reg. Black's Niss worked steadily in the hunt away, slewing well, was under good command, brought back in good style but should have been steadied more. <i>(Jul 23, 1907,Taranaki Herald,8</i>)

>  <b>ACLAND</b> .. When a dog heads or slews sheep, shepherds speak of his having done a good (etc.) <i>turn</i>. <i>(1933,Sheep Station</i>)

>  <i>Sheep dog</i>.- Dog to work sheep; <i>collie</i> (q.v.). <i>S.ds</i>. run naturally either to bring sheep towards you or to drive them away; and when a puppy shows his preference he is broken in for that work. The dogs that bring sheep are called <i>heading ds.</i> (q.v.) and most of these can be taught to<i> lead </i>(q.v.) if desired. Dogs which take to driving sheep away are broken in to<i> huntaway</i> and are called <i>htwys</i> (q.v.). Some dogs will both <i>hd</i>. and <i>htwy</i> and are called <i>handy ds.</i> They are not generally high-class heading dogs but very useful about hand and sometimes very useful mustering dogs. Some men have a special<i> slewing d.</i>, but a well-trained, <i>hdg</i>. dog or <i>htwy</i>. will usually <i>slew </i>(q.v.). (C.) <i>(Nov 25, 1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  <b>CRAWFORD</b> If you `slewed' a mob of strong merino wethers ... <i>(1949,Sheep and Sheepmen of Canterbury,40</i>)

>  <b>HARTLEY</b> <i>Teaching Slewing</i> The next lesson is devised to teach a dog ... to slew sheep. <i>(1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,17</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> <i>Slew</i>: To slew sheep is to turn them in a different direction to that in which they are going. If sheep are sidling round a face and they have to be turned downhill a dog is run out and above them to `slew' them down. <i>(1966,Boss's Story, The,190</i>)

>  <b>McLEOD</b> <i>Slew:</i> A huntaway should be able to cast to the side on command and slew in the desired direction. <i>(1970,Glorious Morning,253</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> A mob of those wethers, slewed out of a high basin, would disappear down a spur in a cloud of dust ... <i>Ibid.</i> 169  <i>Slew</i>: To turn or change the direction in which sheep are travelling. To top-side slew is to turn or hunt them downhill. Slewing is done mainly with huntaways and in one of the huntaways events at our trials - Class III - the sheep are hunted on a zig-zag course. This is often called a slew. <i>(1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,15</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to defeat, overcome, get round (a problem)

>  <b>BUTLER</b> This [waterfall] `stuck us up', as they say here concerning any difficulty. We managed, however, to `slew' it, as they, no less elegantly, say concerning the surmounting of an obstacle. <i>(1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,v 67-68</i>)

### slew round

 
<i>verb</i>. (of bullocks)

>  <b>BUTLER</b> In the small river Ashburton ... we had a little misunderstanding [105] with the bullocks; the leaders ... slewed sharply round and tied themselves into an inextricable knot with the polars [sic] ... <i>(1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,vii 104-105</i>)

>  <b>KENNAWAY</b> ... if he [sc a bullock] pulled up hard and `<i>slewed</i>' sharp round on his heels, the stock-horse would come up standing, just as quickly, and be round on his flank in a second. <i>(1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,206</i>)

### slewer

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] an over-enthusiastic dog that slews sheep [ i.e. turns them in a different direction to that which they should be going. ]

>  <b>STAPLYTON-SMITH</b> Mostly these dogs are of inestimable value, but at times, in an excess of zeal, they may become 'splitters,' or 'slewers' or 'dividers.' <i>(1990,Other End of the Harbour, The,201</i>)

### slewing

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [sheepdogs] the steering of sheep in a particular direction.

>  Class II. - Huntaway, with slew; about quarter of a mile between three sets of flags about two chains apart. Time, 10 minutes. First prize, GBP10; second, GBP6; third, GBP3; fourth, GBP1. Points: Huntaway 10, slewing 10, noise 10, command 5. <i>(May 18, 1904,Otago Witness,50</i>)

>  .. instead of the suggested 25 points for style it would be better to allot them for slewing. <i>(Jan 2, 1941,NZ Farmer,12</i>)

>  <b>HARTLEY</b> In slewing, good clean work, with ample clearance between the dog and sheep is looked for <i>(1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,76</i>)

>  <b>McNAUGHTON</b> Most of the heading and slewing had to be done by Ustice on the hack. <i>(1970,Tat,35</i>)

### slide

 
<i>noun</i>. (mining) a fracture in a lode; a dislocation in a vein etc.

>  FAULT.- A fissure, accompanied by a displacement of the strata, same as a slide, heave, hitch, throw, and trouble. <i>(1868,Thames Miner's Guide, The,54</i>)

>  <b>PYKE</b> That it is a genuine reef, and not a mere `slide', may be regarded as certain. [=? Slicken sides, cf rejects] <i>(1887,Gold Discoveries,15</i>)

>  ... the boreholes projected from the end of the southeast crosscut at No 8 (854 ft.) level reached the unconformity `slide' between the dacites and the barren andesites. <i>(1912,NZ Geol. Survey Bulletin,No 15 (N.S.) 161</i>) [NOTES: (Bell and Fraser) (Waihi-Tairua)]

>  Carbon or carbonaceous material has been observed or detected by analysis in some of the faults (`slides') in the Waihi mine ... <i>(1922,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,5/116</i>) [NOTES: (Morgan)]



 
<i>verb</i>.

See: -

>  Nobody else knows she [a race-horse] can slide <i>(1890,Zealandia,1/488</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a serving hatch

[NOTES: in OED supplement but not in DNZE Slide II.5.j. NZ A serving hatch. **Dictionary search Mar 2006: not Nth Amer, or Austral.]

>  <b>COLE</b> I was standing by the slide in the lounge one night. <i>(1949,It Was So Late,92</i>)

>  Charlie ordered for them both and Kate dragged back to the slide. <i>(1955,Numbers,I(IV) : 14</i>)

>  What happens? Pop-In is very informal. Those who attend are free to come and go as they choose. Sessions begin at 9:30am. Tea, coffee and cordial are available from the kitchen slide from 10am onwards, At about 11am the children are offered a piece of apple and a story is shared. This is followed by music time with musical instruments, action songs and games. <i>(2006,Internet - see Notes</i>) [NOTES: http://tawa-anglican.wellington.net.nz/popin.htmAccessed 20/03/2006. no date for site creation/update.]



 
<i>noun</i>. a slip

>  <b>MAHY</b> It put me back a hundred slides for the heat and beat. <i>(1985,Catalogue of the Universe,49</i>)

>  <b>MICHAEL GROGAN</b> `On the 9th of November, whilst a crowd of diggers were camped on the banks of the Cardrona, Mullins and I took a walk to see how that part of the country looked, and in walking along the river, where what I call a slide had ocurred, there had been a track formed by the cattle. <i>(Nov 9, 1862,Letter</i>) [NOTES: 1862 Nov 9 Michael Grogan in 1863 V. Pyke's Report in 1887 Handbook NZ Mines 9]

>  <b>PYKE</b>  <i>(1887,History of the Early Gold Discoveries  in Otago,82</i>) [NOTES: c1862 Sep in 1887 Pyke History of the Early Gold Discoveries in Otago 1887 (1962) 82]

>  The valley of the Cardrona is characterised by a series of `slides' or landslips. <i>(1863,AJHR,D/6/5</i>) [NOTES: Pyke Goldfields Report]

>  <b>PYKE</b> The valley of the Cardrona is characterised by a number of `slides' or landslips, by some of which the lower strata have been projected to the surface. <i>(1887,History of the Early Gold Discoveries  in Otago,83,1962</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a timber-slide

>  <b>HAY</b> The logs are easily collected ..., as they can be sent down the sides of ranges by means of screw-jacks, rollers and slides. <i>(1882,Brighter Britain,2/11</i>)

### slide (off)

 
<i>verb</i>. to leave, slip away

>  <b>KENNEDY</b> Slide off to your mother, young 'un, and hang yourself up to dry. <i>(1877,Colonial Travel,302</i>)

### sling

 
<i>noun</i>. a payment or bonus; a backhander or bribe

>  And unless the rule is rewritten it would appear licence holders are forbidden to accept slings or to be paid for newspaper tipping columns... If a driver told an owner, or his friend or partner, how he thought his horse would go (or went the previous week) and that person later slung the driver, on the face of it, the  rule was breached. "It must be accepted by HRNZ that for years drivers, trainers and stablehands have accepted by way of a gift a benefit for having provided information." <i>(Jul 27, 2003,Sunday Star Times,B14</i>)

>  How's this for confidence? An owner of a horse racing at Pukekohe on Saturday told a jockey what his `sling' would be for winning. This is the norm, of course. But this fellow told the jockey two races before his steed was to run. The horse was successful and easily too. <i>(Sep 11, 1982,NZ Truth,2</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

See: sc. of wedges

>  <b>R. GILBERD</b> `You'd see the men starting off in the morning to go timber-squaring with a sling of wedges - wedges often had a hole in them so you could tie them each end of a string and sling them over your shoulder.' <i>(Mar 16, 1952,Letter</i>) [NOTES: [ca1880's]]



 
<i>verb</i>. bribe

[NOTES: [cf AND 2. bribe [1875 he'll sling me a tenner] 1905] to pay off, bribe]

>  <b>NEWBOLD</b> SLING (v) Pay off, bribe. <i>(1982,Big Huey, The,253</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to put (a meal) together hastily or carelessly

See: hash-slinger

>  [Diggers out of Uniform Column] `[The Army cooks] didn't serve [food],' said the Grim Dig. `They slung it. Hash-slingers.' <i>(Jun 4, 1955,Upper Hutt Leader,5</i>) [NOTES: cf WF - hash 1929: not specific in P, but perhaps merely an extension of sling = `dispense]

### sling in the mitt

 
<i>phrase</i>. ?variant of throw in the towel

### sling off (at)

 
<i>verb</i>. to jeer (at), mock, make fun (of)

>  Poor Thornton, I should advise you to try to understand a little more clearly what you are writing about next time you start "slinging off" at Dot's correspondents. <i>(Nov 9, 1899,Otago Witness,57</i>)

>  The lawyer, pitying His Honor's ignorance replied that "slinging off" meant "barracking." Even then the judge affected to misunderstand plain English. The lawyer further informed His Honor that "slinging off" meant "against," and "barracking" means "sticking up for." <i>(Mar 28, 1903,NZ Free Lance,14</i>)

>  <b>VIRTUE</b> `... they look like a bunch of bodgies to me. They'll only start slinging off.' <i>(1987,Redemption of Elsdon Bird, The,38,1988</i>)

>  <b>SARGESON</b> `Sketch from Life' They used to sling off at me <i>(1936,Conversations with My Uncle,18</i>)

>  He was always slinging off at everything <i>(1944,NZ New Writing,3/41</i>) [NOTES: G.Lexidor]

>  <b>KIWI</b> They had now altered their time, instead of `slinging off' at the scraggy moke <i>(1911,On the Swag,6</i>)

>  <b>SLATTER</b> Got the pricker with me. Slingin off at me he was. You're up the boo-ay he told me. <i>(1959,Gun in My Hand, A,91</i>)

>  <b>SARGESON</b> sling off at: make fun of, mock. <i>(1964,Collected Stories,303</i>)

>  <i>Sling off:</i> make fun of <i>(1981,Auckland Savings Bank</i>) [NOTES: (Goldie Brown Collection)]

>  <i>sling off vb. (intr., adv.</i>; often foll. by <i>at) Austral. & N.Z. inf.</i> to mock; deride; jeer at. <i>(1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1087</i>) [NOTES: [1986 NZPOD 721; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 456]]

>  Women as a class are not nearly as sensitive as Irishmen about the things "slung off" at them. <i>(Oct 4, 1924,NZ Truth,14</i>)

### slink

 
<i>noun</i>. also called slinkie a) an unborn or stillborn lamb, calf or fawn. b) its skin. a calf or fawn in utero valued for skin markings; a dead lamb (born dead or died soon after birth) which is processed for its skin

>  <b>DAVIN</b> `Ned,' called Paddy, `Sling us up Dad's bike pump, will you?' <i>(1975,Breathing Spaces,17</i>)

>  N.Z. `Slink' In High Demand [heading] ... A coat made from New Zealand `slink' is expected to be shown in the Paris autumn-winter fashion shows, which open here next week. For the uninitiated, `slink' is made from the skins of stillborn lambs. The material is very light and soft, and is highly-prized in the high fashion world of Europe. Each year, apparently, thousands of ewes die before lambing, in the harsh Southland spring. This provides stillborn lambskin which is processed into `slink.' ... <i>(Jul 22, 1971,Otago Daily Times,3</i>) [NOTES: (Griffiths Collection)]

>  <b>THOMPSON</b> The tails were salted as was the `slink' (unborn calf) carcass, while the sinews and antlers in velvet were sun-dried. <i>(1952,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,116</i>)

>  <b>HAYWARD</b> We also called in at a venison-processing plant. In one cool store hung rows of slinks - the bodies of unborn fawns. <i>(Nov 29, 1973,Diary of the Kirk Years,182,1981</i>)

>  Calf or fawn in utero valued for skin markings. <i>Ibid.</i> 51 Slink: Dead lamb (i.e., born or died soon after birth) which is processed for its skin. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,22</i>)

>  <i>slink 2 n. NZ & Austral</i>. still-born lamb or one dead soon after birth, processed for its skin. [orig. = premature calf] <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,721</i>) [NOTES: [cf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict. 1087, sense 4]]



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  The slink skin industry in New Zealand had grown in 10 years to a million dollar export business ... It is an industry born out of the statistical fact that even in ideal climatic conditions 10 per cent of all lambs born each season die at birth. <i>(Sep 19, 1980,Dominion,8</i>)

### slinky

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a skin of a newly born lamb or other animal.

>  The number of slinky skins from dead lambs went up from 700 to 20,000. They didn't have a show. <i>(Sep 13, 1973,NZ Farmer,12</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] an unborn or stillborn lamb.

>  <b>BROSNAHAN</b> Lambing involves low labour inputs with the shepherds going round the Romneys only once a day to pick up slinkies. <i>(1998,Glenaray 1898-1998,83</i>)

>  .. pulling out slinkies (unborn lambs) and trying to revive them with mouth-to-mouth, catching trout with their bare hands ... [slinky skin] <i>(Nov 9, 2002,Dominion Post,A12</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. unborn deer

>  <b>MACNICOL</b> I tanned slinky (unborn deer) hides and nanny-goat skins to make mats. <i>(1965,Skippers Road,47</i>)

### slinter

 
<i>noun</i>. a fast one; modern usage esp. work a slinter [AND A. n. has this 1864 Thatcher cit.]

See: also slanter

[NOTES: The early NZ uses (ca1870-1900) suggest prons. [ lint , slent , lent ], with main senses `crooked', `underhand' `dishonestly tricky' etc, both in general use, and as an adj (? sb as attrib). in racing slang. Sc. dial <i>sklent </i> (sclent) sb (OED) a. Sc. variant of <i>slent </i> sb., a slant or slope; ... a side look etc vb Sc and north dial:1. to move, dart, or fall obliquely; to lie aslant; to give a side-look etc b. fig to deviate from a straightforward course, or from the truth. <i>Slent </i>sb' Now dial. [a ON Slent [a mutation of <i>slant </i>]] 2. on (the) slent aslant. 3. (obs) A sly hit or sarcasm = Slant sb' 5. (1557-1612) vb' Now dial Also 14c. slinte, 15c sclente [a. ON slenta] 1. ... to lie aslant ...]

>  He says when he meets George Dixon it will be no 'slinter,' but a real honest fight. <i>(Apr 2, 1892,Observer (Auckland),11</i>)

>  Most people know that a slinter is aconspiracy ... a take-down. <i>(Jun 22, 1950,Southern Cross (Wgton),11</i>)

>  <b>PASCOE</b> Shearers are still better organized and most sheds have somebody articulate to voice their worries if any `slinters' are feared. <i>(1952,Land Uplifted High,164,1961</i>)

>  <b>MORRIESON</b> So it's the dirtiest lowest crime ..., but what about the slinter they pulled on Granny? Did they show any mercy? <i>(1974,Predicament,74,1981</i>)

>  There is a slinter somewhere - but where? <i>(Nov 23, 1938,Auckland Weekly News,96</i>)

>  Origin only to be guessed at. A false call or call where the driver can't locate the person who ordered the cab. Can be used as a noun - `It's a slinter'; adjectivally - `The slintered car will get the next job'; or as a verb - `I've been slintered'. <i>(Jul 1983,Metro,no.25 81</i>)

>  <b>THATCHER</b> A Lyceum Cafe[e-acute] at the top end was started - / It proved a bad place for the restaurant trade,/ 'Twas a `shlinter' for the tenant one morning departed/ Without paying his rent in the Lowther Arcade./ Lowther Arcade!/ This Le-vite said a-dieu to the Lowther Arcade. <i>(1864,Invercargill Minstrel,15</i>) [NOTES: (The Lowther Arcade)]

>  The controlling officials don't care a dump what the professional stoushers' views may be on the subject; their plain duty will be to protect the public from a recurrence of the `schleinters' which took place in this city in past years. [subject = boxing] <i>(Jul 14, 1906,NZ Truth,56/3/5</i>)

>  The [Boxing] Association is making a `dead set' against the professional talent which has come into such prominence in Wellington of late, and the stoushers' chance of fixing up `shleinter goes' is `Buckley's' <i>(Jul 28, 1906,NZ Truth,58/3/3</i>)

>  Shearers are still better organized and most sheds have somebody articulate to voice their worries if any slinters are feared. <i>(1945,NZ Geographer,24</i>) [NOTES: (Pascoe Canterbury High Country)]

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> A trick, a piece of deceit; esp., work a slinter, to succeed in effecting a trick, a swindle: Australian: C. 20. Baker, 1942 and 1945. cf. Slanter (q.v.), of which it may be a thinned form <i>(1949,Dictionary of the Underworld,638,1961</i>)

>  <b>STEWART</b> `'Strewth, he's a Bobby Dazzler, that one. Liaison business. That's the biggest slinter in the army.' `The biggest which -?' `Slinter. Fiddle. Swan. Look, don't you know?' <i>(1981,Hot & Copper Sky,153</i>)

>  That the Massey Government, or some big military pooh-bah, tried to work a "slinter" on to the poor limbless returned soldiers by offering them a lump sum annually for upkeep of their artificial limbs, instead of, as at present, keeping them in order at the Government's expense. <i>(Jul 3, 1920,NZ Truth,2</i>)

### slintered

 
<i>adjective</i>.

### slip

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [stock sales] a young pig.

>  Livestock sales: big slips 16/- to 17/-. <i>(May 1909,NZ Farmer,408</i>)

>  The usual practice is to buy the pigs as slips. <i>(Dec 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,559</i>)

>  Slips and weaners have been in demand. <i>(Aug 16, 1951,NZ Farmer,43</i>)

>  Weaners and slips have fluctuated somewhat, the trend being downwards during the first week of the fortnight. <i>(Oct 9, 1952,NZ Farmer,40</i>)

>  A pig underfed in the early stages of growth (particularly as a weaner and a slip) and then 'given the works' with a cheap food is likely to produce an unsatisfactory pork chop. <i>(Sep 10, 1970,NZ Farmer,67</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a gouging of a slope or hillside through water erosion.

>  <b>DARE</b> There had been several slips during the recent heavy rains ... <i>(1956,Rouseabout Jane,20</i>)

>  SLIP ON RIMUTAKA-ROAD. .. It will take two or three weeks to clear the slip away, and the earth is still coming ... <i>(Jul 6, 1910,Evening Post,8</i>)

>  The party of men engaged on the Haven Road were digging down a portion of the hill near the Custom House, for the purpose of getting materiel [sic] for the surface of this excellent work, when a slip took place which completely buried Keats, and fell also on two others named Sharman and Mansell. <i>(Mar 11, 1843,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,210</i>)

>  <b>MCCASKILL</b> .. in the Whangamomona-Ohura inland the deforested hillsides are maimed with scars produced by mass movements of varied morphology: they are, however, known universally in New Zealand as slips. <i>(1973,Hold This Land,40</i>)

>  <b>MCCASKILL</b> No study of the distribution or mechanics of 'slips' has been undertaken ... <i>(1973,Hold This Land,41</i>)

>  <b>BRADSHAW & WILLIAMS</b> A number [of farmers] quoted figures such as slips only recover to 80% of production over 20 years and grass on slipped areas go into drought stress three days after slipping. However, many agree that intuitively they know there are costs involved in continuing to farm these areas as well as the loss of grass growth on slips. <i>(1998,Information and Communication Needs,25</i>)

>  The rapidity of the water undermines the latter, and occasions frequent slips. <i>(Sep 12, 1840,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [stock] to lose weight or some aspect of condition; to revert or regress.

>  <b>STEVENS</b> .. the shepherd who observes after a change of paddocks or a bad break of weather, 'Ewes aren't milking and the lambs have slipped' has at least his eyes on his job. <i>(1958,Sheep.  Part 1, Sheep husbandry,62</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [ dog trials] to liberate sheep used in a trial.

>  <b>GORDON</b> .. in the South island, liberating is called slipping, which means they slip sheep on to the mark, using slippers. <i>(1998,Three Sheep and a Dog,196</i>)

>  But the cunning sheep do not always want to be "slipped" away from their woolly mates. <i>(Apr 19, 2001,Taranaki Daily News,19</i>)

### slip bar

 
<i>noun</i>.

See: slip-panel, slip-rail

[NOTES: aka slip-bar]

>  Mr. J. W. Baker wrote complaining of slip bars and log fence across Climie road. This was a case of two neighbors disagreeing as to cattle running on adjacent clearings. <i>(Mar 10, 1882,Hawera & Normanby Star,2</i>)

### slip rail

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] the rail of a post-and-rail fence or gate which can be slid back to reveal an opening.

[NOTES: aka slip-rail; also Aust; also figurative]

>  <b>BARKER</b> ... they all trotted into the stockyard ...and I had nothing to do but put up the slip-rail as fast as I could ... <i>(1868,Station Life in NZ,234,1870</i>)

>  <b>LADY BARKER</b> He bounded over the slip-rail of the paddock before Karl could get it down. We were too primitive for gates in those parts <i>(1873,Station Amusements in NZ,68</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> part of a fence so fitted that it can be removed so as to serve as a gate,. Used also for the gateway thus formed. Generally in the plural. Same as <i>Slip-panel. [1870] <i>(1898,Austral English,420</i>)

>  <b>HENDERSON</b> SLIP RAIL: Slips easily into holes in posts and two or three act as a gate. <i>(1961,Friends in Chains,189</i>) [NOTES: c1900-1920 A Teamster's Glossary in 1961 Henderson Friends In Chains 189]

>  As for the colonial slip-rail, it is an abomination ... <i>(1902,Brett's Colonists Guide,96</i>)

>  The old devil father ... took Inias horse, put him outside the boundary, wired up the slip rails and padlocked the gate. <i>(Aug 26, 1903,Chudleigh Diary,419,1950</i>)

>  <b>BAUCKE</b> From the front door a plain, weedless pathway ... leads down an easy grade to the front gate (slip-rails). <i>(1905,Where the White Man Treads,296</i>)

>  <b>SATCHELL</b> Lena made no reply, but when the slip-rail was reached she looked quickly at er companion. <i>(1905,Toll of the Bush,31,1985</i>)

>  They then got through the slip rails close to Himeonas camp and mounted their horses before Himeonas party saw them. <i>(Jul 8, 1912,Chudleigh Diary,457,1950</i>)

>  <b>LANCASTER</b> The whare, and the young trees, and the slip-rails, where the cows stood lowing, ... <i>(1930,NZ Short Stories,74</i>)

>  <i>slip-rail</i>: fence with rail which can be slipped out to make gateway. <i>(1947,Reeds' School Dictionary: NZ Suppl.,175</i>)

>  <b>SCANLAN</b> For an hour Ambrose smoked his pipe as he leant over the slip-rail behind the cow-bails; ... <i>(1948,Dusty Road,81,1949</i>)

>  Part of a fence, usually two rails so fitted that they can be easily removed to serve as a gate. <i>(1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),372</i>)

>  <i>slip-rail n. </i>[usually in plural] panels of fence which can be removed to serve as a gate; the gateway itself. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625</i>)

>  <i>sliprail n.</i> (usually in plural) panels of fence which can be removed to serve as a gate; gateway itself. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18</i>)

>  <i>sliprail n. NZ & Austral. </i>fence-rail forming one of a set which can be slipped out to make an opening. <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,722</i>) [NOTES: [cf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict. 1088; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 456]]

>  <b>RICHARDS</b> Most of the gateways were either `Taranakis' or slip-rails ... <i>(1986,Off the Sheep's Back,103</i>)

>  <b>KOEBEL</b> Their eyes roam from their horses to the timber of some slip-rails in the wire-fencing. <i>(1905,Return of Joe,228</i>)

>  In the end we had to grease all the wires and prise him through with a sliprail. <i>(Jul 11, 1910,Triad, The,XVIII(4) : 20</i>)

>  The long summer morning's muster, beginning before the dark, has finally ended at about 11 a.m. with the big herd of cows and calves safely confined behind the slip rails of the receiving yard. <i>(Mar 23, 1967,NZ Farmer,33</i>)

>  <b>RICHARDS</b> Most of the gateways were either 'Taranakis' or slip-rails. [slip-rail] <i>(1986,Off the Sheep's Back,103</i>)

>  She saw him lying down near the slip rails.. The slip rails were down when I got there. <i>(Jul 2, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,20</i>)

>  Our son.. calls our place "Sledge - andSliprail Farm." <i>(Feb 26, 1926,North & South,38</i>)

>  The main point in Smith's story - and he made the rails of the witness-box a convenient substitute for his homestead slip-rails in its telling - was that in March last Wilson was supposed to have insinuated to his (Smith's) son that some couple of dozen head of Wanaka station sheep had been shorn in Smith's shed. <i>(Nov 22, 1928,NZ Truth,5</i>)

>  You'll meet me at the slip-rails when thecoach comes this evening. <i>(Nov 18, 1899,NZ Times,3</i>)

>  <b>SCANLON</b> For an hour Ambrose smoked his pipe as he leaned over the slip-rail behind the cow-bails. <i>(1948,Rusty Road,81</i>)</i>

### slipe

 
<i>noun</i>. farming: wool recovered from pelts in an abattoir or freezing works; wool recovered from pelts in an abbatoir by a wool puller after being chemically loosened with a sodium sulphide and hydrated lime mixture

>  The chemical action of this solution loosens the wool from the skin, and it is easily plucked off by hand. The wool (called `slipe') is then dried and packed in bales for shipment; the skin (now called `pelt') is washed, skivered, and finally pickled ... <i>(1918,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,1/165</i>)

>  <i>Slipe</i>: Wool recovered from pelts in abbatoir. Body wool typed as woolly lambs, shorn lambs, and sheep. Oddments typed as seconds, thirds, and slipemaster. <i>Ibid.</i> <i>Slipe</i>: Wool recovered by a wool puller, chemically loosened with a sodium sulphide and hydrated lime mixture. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,59</i>)

>  <i>slipe n. N.Z. 1.</i> wool removed from the pelt of a slaughtered sheep by immersion in a chemical bath. <i>2. (as modifier): slipe wool.</i> [C14 in England: <i> slype</i>  to strip, skin] [? cognate with <i>slip, slippery</i>] <i>(1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1088</i>) [NOTES: [1986 NZPOD 722; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 456]]

>  Skin and slipe 1s 2 1/2 d to 1s 4d ... <i>(Aug 20, 1842,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3</i>) [NOTES: (Extract from the <i>New Zealand Monthly Magazine, 3,</i> 1842-)]

>  The number of bales of New Zealand wool were 1,968; the prices realized were as follows:- Fleeces, 1s. 1d. to 1s. 10d .. slipe and skin, 1s. to 1s. 4 1/2 d. <i>(May 9, 1855,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2</i>)

>  Wool reports of the sales June 28 to 30, received by the San Francisco mail, show the following averages: Kapai clip, 106 bales greasy, average sixpence and seven-tenths .. Tora, 178 bales greasy 6 4-9d, 28 scoured, slipe, and washed 7 3-7d ... <i>(Aug 8, 1898,Poverty Bay Herald,3</i>)

>  45 bales slipe wool, valued at [GBP]582. <i>(Jul 4, 1889,Hawke's Bay Herald,2</i>)

>  Medium were from par to 5 per cent. lower, shabby 5 per cent. lower, scoureds and slipes 5 per cent. lower, merinos par to 5 per cent. lower. <i>(Mar 8, 1923,Evening Post,7</i>)

>  Slipes, medium to coarse crossbred, advanced 5 per cent., and fine wool slipes were 10 per cent. higher. <i>(Jul 6, 1932,Evening Post,12</i>)



 
<i>adjective</i>. [Rural] [of sheep] with a fleece of 25 to 50 cm length of wool [ that can be sliped off after slaughter.]

>  Medium slipe ewes $20-$21 .. slipe lambs $27.20 ... <i>(Jul 6, 1995,NZ Farmer,39</i>)

>  Prime sheep: top slipe ewes $76-$80.20 .. hvy slipe lambs $112-$116. <i>(Aug 14, 2001,Dominion,6</i>)

>  Stortford Lodge price range .. hvy slipe ewes $73-%76.50; slipe male lambs $112-$117. <i>(Aug 21, 2001,Dominion,8</i>)

>  Slipe ewes $68.70 - $73.75. <i>(Mar 19, 2002,Hawke's Bay Today,11</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to pull or peel wool from a sheep skin.

>  <b>PRESTON</b> The pelts [of the frozen sheep] were completely useless: but the wool sliped off was just as good as any other wool. <i>(1978,Woolgatherers,111</i>)

>  <b>WONZ</b> At the freezing works pelts from slaughtered lambs are treated with a chemical enabling ther wool to be plucked or 'sliped' from the skin. <i>(1980,NZ Sheep and Their Wool,ii</i>)

<i>noun</i>. a sledge

<i>verb</i>. to draw or carry on a sledge N.I.

### slipe wool

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] raw wool that has been removed from a sheep skin after it has died or been slaughtered.

<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>BREMNER</b> <i>Slipewool</i> Wool removed from sheepskins by fellmongers. <i>(1985,Woolscours of NZ,10</i>)

### slipemaster

 
<i>noun</i>. a class of wool recovered by a slipemaster

>  <i>Slipe</i>: Wool recovered from pelts in abbatoir. Body wool typed as woolly lambs, shorn lambs, and sheep. Oddments typed as seconds, thirds, and slipemaster. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,59</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a machine used to recover wool from pelt trimmings in a fellmongery

>  <b>MORRIESON</b> He had expected to find Entwistle standing at the bend of one of the slipe masters, the machines which had replaced the outcast but fabulously paid gang of men whose job had been to save the precious strands of wool after maggots had devoured the adhering meat. ... This wool was thrown into baskets. <i>(1976,Pallet on the Floor,94</i>)

>  <i>Slipemaster</i>: Machine used to recover wool from pelt trimmings in a fellmongery <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,62</i>)

### slipper

 
<i>verb</i>. to beat; to best

<i>noun</i>.

### sluice

 
<i>verb</i>. in phr. get sluiced out: to get washed out

>  <b>PYKE</b> See here, our claim is a mighty small part of them beaches, and if we get sluiced out of one, we can darned soon get another. <i>(1873,Wild Will Enderby,1/viii/31,(1889,1974)</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. 1. a channel which carries or controls a flow of water. Short form of sluiceway. 2. a gate or valve used to control such a flow. sluice, verb, to send a stream of water out, over or through.

>  Their sluice has a fall or grade of about 1 in 22 1/2, and the Kumara Channel 1 in 26. <i>(Aug 3, 1883,West Coast Times,2</i>)

>  THE DEPOSITION OF GOLD IN RIVERS indicates that the metal must have been native to its banks, and washed down to lower levels as the rivers deepened their beds. In proof of this it may be mentioned that had the gold been fed into the watercourses at their heads the heavier gold would be found in its upper portions, the lighter and finer gold lower down the stream, and that the very fine gold had travelled the greatest distance; and such is found to be the case in all artificial sluices and tail races. <i>(May 8, 1890,Otago Witness,13</i>)

>  The men are satisfied with the amount of gold found [in Otago] though it is not of a very good [40] quality, too fine, not nuggety enough to use a sluice well so they adopt the slower and surer way of cradling. <i>(May 23, 1862,Chudleigh Diary,39,1950</i>)

>  <b>CAPT. ANDERSON</b> They have succeeded in forming a small race by which they are enabled to form a sluice. Mr W. Parker produced a parcel of gold (five ounces) the proceeds of one day's work of his party of five. <i>(Jul 26, 1863,Letter</i>) [NOTES: 1863 July 26 Capt Anderson in 1948 Cowan Down the Years in the Maniototo 38]

>  <b>MONEY</b> Meanwhile, our Oxonian `chips' had prepared three boxes or sluices, open at both ends, each 12 feet in length, 2 in width, and 1 in depth ... <i>(1871,Knocking About in NZ,16</i>)

>  <i>Sluice</i>: A long trough along which the wash-dirt is forced by a stream of water leaving behind the metallic particles which are caught by the riffles. <i>(1935,Gold Mining Year Book,11</i>)

>  We christened the sluice at Hohonu, / and all the "Big Bugs from Uskub" were there, / So we guzzled and jossed at the shareholders' cost, / While the "Bon-Ton" were hugging the Bear / The Hohonu Tame Bear. <i>(Dec 4, 1915,Grey River Argus,7</i>)

>  If wrought from the surface down, and washed by a Tom or sluice, wages might be made. <i>(Jan 28, 1885,Nelson Examiner,2</i>)

>  ".. The lure of gold brought the blue-shirted diggers up this way just on seventy years ago, and many a place name about the lake is a relic of those days of wash-dish and sluice ..." <i>(Nov 5, 1929,Evening Post,10</i>)

### slush lamp

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [used elsewhere but recorded earliest in NZ] a basic light source, being a tin filled with fat in which a wick is placed.

>  <b>BIDWILL & WOODHOUSE</b> The working men's quarters were lighted by "slush" lamps, made by placing a twisted rag in the centre of a small tin of fat. <i>(1927,Bidwill of Pihautea,14</i>)

>  Slush lamps... consisted of a small tin of fat into which a piece of rag or wick had been placed. <i>(1988,Tales of Pioneer Women,312</i>) [NOTES: Writing of 1940]

>  In other times he used a slush lamp for artificial light. <i>(Oct 14, 1953,NZ Observer,16</i>)

>  The slush lamp was alight when found by the police. <i>(May 18, 1936,Evening Post,11</i>)

The rag is lit with a match or a stick from the fire; the wick is fed by the surrounding fat, and the surrounding darkness is made visible. <i>(1875,Adventuring in Maoriland in the Seventies,30,1935</i>) [NOTES: 1872 Oct in c1875 Meredith Adventuring in Maoriland (1935) 30]

### smallfarmer

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  What, then, is a smallfarmer? "A vertically challenged agriculturalist," runs the well-worn joke. While names like "smallholder" or the American "homesteader" might be less obvious butts, they are really no more descriptive. "Toy farmer" is obviously derisive, while "hobby farmer" rather unfairly equates small-scale farming with stamp collecting or restoring old cars. <i>Ibid.</i> 42 John Fairweather.. defines smallfarmers (or smallholders, as he categorises them) as people who have  a commitment to effective land use, and who earn at least some farm income. They differ from a group he calls "lifestylers" - a term derived from the ubiquitous "life style block" dreamed up by real-estate agents when they began to sell the concept of country living 20 years ago. <i>(Jan 2000,NZ Geographic,No. 45/41</i>)

>  <b>McLAGLAN</b> In the course of time work on certain unforeseen activities accrued to the School Medical Service. There were, for instance, the many special investigations undertaken by S.M.O.s throughout New Zealand. <i>(1965,Stethoscope & Saddlebags,148</i>)

### smoke

 
<i>verb</i>. to hide

>  They were talking about the watch and `Spider,' Warren, and James said they got it from an old man at the Royal Hotel. Warren said he had the chain and `smoked' it. After that James and Ted pawned the watch, ... <i>(Apr 16, 1910,NZ Truth,251/5/5</i>)

### smoke (off)

 
<i>verb</i>. to depart, get going; to depart hastily and unobtrusively; to shoot through

See: -

[NOTES: Jim Cameron writes: NSOD gives this as <i>Austral.</i>. Not in Cassells. No NZ dictionary  entry but I have heard it occasionally since the 50s.]

>  <i>smoke v..i. sl. </i>to escape; to run away. <i>(1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,11</i>)

>  <i> v.int. smoke </i> to decamp escape: (phrase) in smoke, usually of criminals in hiding. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625</i>)

>  Lawyer Hindmarsh protested that the warrant was a high-handed proceeding, while Mr Dix, on the other hand, declared that he had ample evidence to show that Sarah intended `smoking off.' <i>(Sep 24, 1910,NZ Truth,274/7/4</i>)

>  <b>SYDER & HODGETTS</b> To depart unobtrusively. .in 4;`I don't see him - he was here a few minutes ago. He must have smoked off somewhere.' <i>(1974,Australian & NZ English [TS],966</i>)

### smoker

 
<i>noun</i>. a little pink sweet, size of aspirin, with a musky taste or perfume, perhaps originally meant to take the smell of smoking from the breath. Jane Godfrey notes that the names is still current, and the sweets still available at Woolworths

<i>noun</i>. a handpiece for a shearing machine

<i>noun</i>. a smoke concert

### smokies

 
<i>noun</i>. opaque brown and grey marbles; also called OYSTERS [OED[S] check

[NOTES: 1945 Baker Aust. Lay. 204 ca1950's Naenae, Wellington (p.c. G. Kennedy)]

>  <b>de MAUNAY</b> Once he gave him a bag of marbles, good ones, too, "smokies", not the useless little clay things. <i>(1949,Huntsman in His Career, The,136</i>)

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as `taw' or `shooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; `dubs', `dates', `stakes', `dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,174</i>)

>  <b>KEITH & MAIN</b> Marbles were the currency of childhood and there were an astonishing number of names for them, some referring to the material or colour, others to value or function in the game. There were agates, aggies, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cats-eye, [sic] chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, mollies, peelies, peewees, pisswees, pretties, Scotties, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers and whities. The march of technology added ball bearings - ballies or steelies - which were unbeatable when it came to smashing an opponent's miserable glassie. World War II[roman] brought `clayeys' often imperfectly spherical they were pathetic terracotta substitutes for real marbles. <i>(1984,NZ Yesterdays,288</i>)

### smoking

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] the pacifying of wild animals with smoke.

>  <b>RICHARDS</b> Before releasing the wild cattle from the yards, in preparation for the 40-mile trip they were given a good 'smoking' to help subdue them. Several fires of green manuka twigs and leaves were lit around the yard and the cattle came through the smoky haze docile and subdued. <i>(1989,Pioneer Family, A,49</i>)

### smother

 
<i>noun</i>.

[NOTES: 1933 see cit. v1]

>  Dangers of a 'smother' are real <i>(1945,NZ Geographer,1/27</i>)

>  [check whether this refers to <i>smother </i>] <i>(1966,NZ Short Stories,210</i>) [NOTES: 1963 Middleton in 1966 NZ Short Stories 210]

>  <b>MACNICOL</b> ... a large mob of sheep was allowed to mass on the road too quickly. This resulted in a `smother', the dread of all sheep-meu, and about sixty corpses were thrown over the edge of the road. ... <i>(1965,Skippers Road,141</i>)

>  <b>BURDON</b> Difficulties arose only when they [sc. Merinos] started to go in the wrong direction and had to be stopped, or when a large mob was in hand and a steep, narrow gully had to be crossed; then there was always the danger of a `smother'. <i>(1938,High Country,108</i>)

>  <b>STUDHOLME</b> The third day, as the sheep mobbed up, it was necessary to exercise great care in running a dog, for a rough turn could cause a bolt, or even a smother, if a deep gut came in the way. ... As soon as the whole mob was in hand and had been given a few turns, the danger of a smother lessened. <i>(1940,Te Waimate,123,1954</i>)

>  <b>BLAKISTON</b> If such a mob runs into a steep-sided gully, they are likely to pile up at the bottom until those behind are running across a bridge of bodies, and, in hundreds, are suffocated. Shepherds dread a `smother', <i>(1952,My Yesteryears,20</i>) [NOTES: [f. c1869]]

>  <b>McLEOD</b> Shepherds dread a `smother' ... <i>(1972,High Country Anthology,80</i>) [NOTES: 1972 Blakiston `Sheep Station Life' in 1972 McLeod High Country Anthology 80]

>  <b>CRUMP</b> I've been off water for years, ever since we had a smother up the back and the creek ran dry before it came down in a stinking flood. <i>(1962,One of Us,88</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  The rider of Nukuhan was in sore straits in the Scurry at Taranaki, as his instructions were to give the chestnut a good smother. Across the bottom bend he was on the outer, but then he came in to the rails, and despite the boy's efforts, he finished second. <i>(Feb 26, 1910,NZ Truth,244/2/7</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a suffocation of sheep, usually en masse [ when driven hard downhill or near water, or worried in a paddock by a dog and being forced together into a tight pack. ]

>  <b>ACLAND</b> They had a bad smother there. <i>(1930,Early Canterbury Runs,128</i>)

>  <b>BLAKISTON</b> Shepherds dread a 'smother' and when the last creek was crossed, and the sheep safe in a holding paddock we were all very pleased. <i>(1952,My Yesteryears,20</i>)

>  <b>GASCOIGNE</b> A smother like this is news and you'll be branded a bad shepherd and me a worse owner. A smother is one of the easiest things in the world to happen with sheep if the conditions are there, and we made them, in the first place by running a fence through that hole. <i>(1965,From the Top of a Hill,125</i>)

>  <b>KERR</b> They [Merinos] roamed far in the days before fences, and mustering was difficult. The new chum found to his cost that 'they'd rush for miles at the sound of a bark, and you would have a pile up and a smother on your hands.' <i>(1976,From the Beginning: chronicles of a county,131</i>)

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> smother: if sheep are bustled into any sort of a defile it only needs one of them to stumble and it will trip others. In next to no time there can be the dreadful and awful sight of a mass of struggling mutton, feet high. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,74</i>)

>  <b>WATT</b> Bad handling can cause many problems and one of these is smother. <i>(1990,Wild Horses & Me,150</i>)

>  <b>STACEY</b> Care had to be taken there to prevent a big smother in the bog. <i>(1996,Tales of a Tussock Jumper,83</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [sheep]  to suffocate when pushed together too closely.

>  PHARAZYN Journal Han 15 152 Teddy and W. to lambs to drive them to pen, smothered 10 in a blind gully ... <i>(1848</i>)

>  <b>CHAMIER</b> There's half a dozen sheep worried and a hundred smothered in the Great Gap ... <i>(1891,Philosopher Dick,248</i>)

>  <b>MILLS ET AL</b> As shown by their speed and activity lambs are very susceptible to fright and are likely to pile up and smother at the slightest provocation. <i>(1964,Practical Guide to Handling Dogs and Stock,79</i>)

>  <b>HALL</b> The man on the bottom beat got into trouble. Some sheep had been smothered through a bit of poor shepherding ... <i>(1987,Shepherd's Year, A,84</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. see cit. 1933

See: -

>  There were <i>only ten</i> sheep smothered during the day. <i>(Mar 1, 1885,Wairarapa Daily,2</i>)

>  <b>FORD</b> Aitken left a mob of sheep run [on] a wrong spur and smothered a large number ... [sic] <i>(Jan 10, 1867,Diary</i>) [NOTES: 1867 Jan 10 Ford Diary in 1981 Crawford Station Years 181]

>  <b>OGONOWSKA-COATES</b> <i>Smother </i>. If the pens in a woolshed are filled too tight sheep may smother during the night. Sheep are kept in the pens overnight before they are shorn. <i>(1987,Boards, Blades & Barebellies,97</i>)

>  <i>Smother.</i>- Run sheep especially merinos, are very easy to s. on broken hill ground. An injudicious turn with a dog in an abrupt gully may stop the lead and cause some sheep to be knocked over. Other sheep make a rush and are brought down too, so that in a second or two there is struggling heap; and before the shepherd can pull them off one another the bottom ones are <i>smothered </i>. They <i> sd.</i> 1200 once on the Stew Point country at Mount Peel, and I believe there was a still worse <i> s </i>. on a station called Roxburgh in Otago. People who fill their woolsheds too tight often <i>smother </i> sheep on a smaller scale: perhaps half a dozen or so in a night. (C.) <i>(Dec 2, 1933,Press, The</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  <b>BURDON</b> Difficulties arose only when they started to go in the wrong direction and had to be stopped, or when a large mob was in hand and a steep, narrow gully had to be crossed; then there was always the danger of a `smother.' Of all breeds the Merino is the easiest to smother, for he moves freer, faster, and more recklessly than any other. If pressed or carelessly handled, some of the leaders may fall or be knocked over and those behind will pile up on top of them until the gully is filled level to the top with struggling sheep. <i>(1938,High Country,108</i>)

>  <b>PHARAZYN</b> to lambs to drive them to pen, smothered 10 in a blind gully. <i>(Jan 15, 1848,Journal,97</i>) [NOTES: (also 152 chk) Teddy and W. [some of cit missing???]]

>  In a minute half the mob were in. We pushed our horses in and prevented the others from going in. [36] If they had 3 out of 4 would have been smothered. <i>(May 2, 1862,Chudleigh Diary,35,1950</i>)

### smother weed

### smothering

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] the suffocating of sheep when forced together in a close mob.

>  It is undesirable to have yards on a very steep slope, as the danger of smothering, particularly with lambs in a large yard, is greatly increased. <i>(Jul 5, 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,2</i>)

>  <b>BOWEN</b> The 'sheepo' must keep an eye on them for smothering, the first sign of which is sheep jumping into a pen. <i>(1956,Wool Away!,iv 47</i>)

>  <b>GORDON</b> One of the biggest risks in high country shepherding is smothering. This can occur at difficult crossings, gateways or narrow gullies, where stock can stumble and go under. 'Smothering can be a problem with Merinos.' Other causes of smothering can be thoughtless shepherding or a dog that decided to ignore its stop whistle. <i>(1987,People, Places & Paddocks,42</i>)

>  <b>BARDSLEY</b> Five hundred [wethers] were lost through smothering and the Air Force compensated the station ... <i>(2000,Land Girls, The,98</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

<i>noun</i>. a sixpence

<i>noun</i>. any of a group of edible pinkish-white fish found in Australian and New Zealand waters; also spelt incorrectly schnapper; also called tamure

>  <b>POLACK</b> ... the fisherman had been successful, producing ... snapper fish, and the kawai [a1-acute], a species of colourless salmon. <i>(1838,New Zealand (various authors/titles),1/198</i>)

>  <b>POLACK</b> Many other fish are equally numerous, answering to our <i>hakes, tench, bream, snapper, haddock, elephant-fish, pollock, salmon, gurnards, pipe-fish, parrot-fish, leather-jackets, cole-fish, John Dorys, sword-fish, cod </i>; various kinds of <i> skate </i> and <i>cat-fish, sting-ray </i> and <i>dog-fish </i>. <i>(1838,New Zealand (various authors/titles),1/322</i>)

>  <b>POLACK</b> Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called para[as-acute] <i>paraua </i>[a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale,<i> mungu nui </i> (black physeter); right whale,<i> tohora </i> (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, <i>mango </i> (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, mpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. <i>(1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/202fn</i>)

### Snares crested penguin

 
<i>noun</i>. [Environment]

>  The islands' only endemic seabird is the Snares crested penguin, which stands a little less than knee high and has a jazzy yellow head-crest, a tangerine-coloured bill, pink feet and smart black-and-white plumage. (A small number of birds display a phenomenon called isabellinism, in which the back feathers are pale fawn).<i>Ibid.</i> 66 [Hdg] Like corks in a maelstrom, Snares crested penguins bob about in the churning surf waiting for a wave to lift them onto shore... Snares crested penguins are one of four species of crested penguins - three of them endemic - which breed in New Zealand waters. All possess a pair of distinctive bands called supercilliary stripes, which run from the bill to the back of the head like giant yellow eyebrows... When the feathers are dry, the bands fluff out to create the classic crested-penguin "punk rocker" look... <i>(Mar 2003,NZ Geographic,62/65</i>)

>  These [birds] include the Snares crested penguins, which raise their young in densely crowded colonies from late August to February each year, competing with millions of other seabirds for food. <i>(Mar 18, 1984,Listener (New Zealand Listener),81</i>)

>  Each island group has its own penguin species, erect-crested, yellow-eyed, Snares crested, gentoo and rock hopper. <i>(Mar 18, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),26</i>)

### snark

 
<i>noun</i>. a portable black box which contains a radio receiver, data logger and special computer software package

[NOTES: does not appear to be an acronym]

>  A radio transmitter recorder ("snark") is placed in the areas where males repeatedly emit their low frequency boom... When kakapo pass a "snark", it detects the radio frequency from each bird's transmitter. <i>(May 8, 2005,Sunday Star Times,A8</i>)

>  The innovation centres around a portable black box, known as a 'Snark', which contains a radio receiver, data logger and special computer software package. Once placed in the forest, the Snark records the movements of any birds within, say, a 10 metre radius and stores this on its memory. Staff can then come along with a portable mini-computer, plug it into the Snark, and find out what birds have been in the area overnight. <i>(Jan 14, 2006,Dominion Post</i>) [NOTES: http://www.kakaporecovery.org.nz/what/technology.htmlaccessed 14/01/2006Latest website updates: 19 September 2005]

### snib

>  Thus <i>snib</i> exists both as noun and as verb. The little lever on the lock is described as the 'snib', and 'snibbed' is used to describe the state of the lock. >  <i>Snib</i> is alive and well in Australia, where it keeps doors closed securely. It can be used as a noun referring to the mechanism which works only from one side of a door in a Yale-type lock and fixes the door closed, or to a latch; and as a verb meaning to engage the mechanism or latch. <i>(Oct 2000,NZWords,4 : 3</i>)
