From a hidden and remote distance a human voice gave a ... cry. [102] `That's the snigger,' Sandy said. <i>(1981,Black Beech & Honeydew,101</i>)

>  Following are the daily rates .. panners-off, motormen, sniggers, bush winchmen, and tractor drivers, 18s ... <i>(Sep 24, 1936,Evening Post,7</i>)

### snigging

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] the hauling of heavy loads of flax, wood or tree-stumps with a snig-chain and horse, bullock, or, more recently, tractor.

>  During the last week four men working making sledge track to suspension brdge, snigging material, and shifting poles and transformer from old incline drive and re-erecting at new incline shaft site. <i>(Dec 21, 1933,Evening Post,14</i>)

>  Sleeper-cutters seem to have practically cut out the whole of this timber within reasonable distance or horse tracks of roads, and in doing so have destroyed millions of young seedling trees in "snigging" or in sqaring ports or sleepers, and then putting a match to the tops and chips. <i>(Sep 5, 1906,Otago Witness,17</i>)

>  Mr Peattie, the proprietor of the section in which one of them is built, requires compensation for right of access before he allows us to put timber on the ground. In the meantime I have had it stacked on the side of the main road ready for snigging when Mr Peattie is arranged with. <i>(Nov 15, 1879,North Otago Times,2</i>)

>  From the nature of the work these horses have been occupied in they are especially suitable for logging, snigging and general saw-milling work. <i>(Apr 21, 1899,West Coast Times,3</i>)

>  "Sawmilling. - Very busy. Men for breaking down, snigging, tram-laying and slabbying are being advertised for ..." <i>(Feb 5, 1916,Grey River Argus,5</i>)

>  Tenders for snigging or carting 50 tons of rails, close at this office at 6 o'clock this evening. <i>(Jun 11, 1887,West Coast Times,2</i>)

>  But silver pine, as everyone knows, grows principally on the Pakihis, from which the sleepers can only be got out of by means of "snigging," the ground being soft, almost swampy. <i>(Apr 2, 1901,Grey River Argus,2</i>)

>  <b>MOWAT</b> In afternoon got 3 snigs of wood ready for snigging. <i>(May 8, 1907,Alexander Mowat Diaries</i>)

>  <b>JOHNSTON</b> In the early days the flax was pulled to load sites by a single draught-horse, which was called "snigging" .. Snigging: this involved pulling flax out of the gullies to a loading site. <i>(1990,Redan, Valley of Farming and Flaxmilling,164</i>)

>  They have cost me L1 1s each; snigging between Queenstown and Arthur's Point, has cost me 15s a post, and there has been the 6s 6d for erecting, superintendence being in all cases excluded. <i>(Jul 1, 1864,Otago Daily Times,4</i>)

>  <b>MALFROY</b> OPERATION COSTS ... (a) Felling (b) ... (c) Snigging or skidding <i>Ibid.</i>39 Snigging .. The pulling of a log endwise along the ground by wire-rope haul, bullock-team, or other power. In America called `skidding.' <i>(1923,Small Sawmills,8</i>)

>  <b>SARGESON</b> (gloss.) snigging: a method of draggging logs without te use of a sledge. </i>Ibid.</i>279 Snigging: method of dragging posts or logs without a sledge. <i>(1949,I Saw in My Dream,273,1974 ed. Rhodes</i>)

>  <i>Snigging </i>: Log haulage. <i>(1953,NZ Forest Glossary</i>)

>  <b>OWEN & PERKINS</b> It was astonishing the tremendous loads they could pull out of the bush along the ground - `snigging', that was called. In many places the logs were brought out on what was called a `cat', which was short for catamaran. A catamaran was a big heavy sledge made of bush timber ... The bushmen would build a special road for them - a corduroy road, or `skidded' road, as we used to call it. <i>(1986,Speaking for Ourselves,160</i>) [NOTES: (Joe Gasparich, Northland kauri country)]

>  This is done by a low or high lead and is called "snigging". <i>(1944,Korero (AEWS Background Bulletin),2(9) : 25</i>)

>  I got mine snigging <i>(Jan 10, 1947,Listener (New Zealand Listener),23</i>) [NOTES: Republished in 1953 NZ Short Stories 371]

>  SNIPE: To round off the end of a log in order to avoid snigging. <i>(Sep 1958,NZ Timber Journal,87</i>)

### snipe

 
<i>noun</i>. a bird

>  <b>GUTHRIE-SMITH</b> The species we hoped to make friends with [off Stewart Island] were the Snipe (<i>Gallinaga Aucklandica </i>), the South Island Crow (<i>Glaucopis cinerea </i>), and the South Island Thrush (<i>Turnagra crassirostris </i>). <i>(1936,NZ Naturalist,175</i>)

>  <b>FALLA et al.</b> Godwits are sometimes referred to as `snipe' or `curlew'. Both these names are quite incorrect. <i>(1966,Birds of New Zealand,116</i>)

>  <b>NATUSCH</b> [Only one of the 18 Northern Hemisphere nesting migratory birds], the snipe (<i>Coenocorypha aucklandica </i>) is a true New Zealander <i>(1967,Animals of NZ, The,262</i>)

>  <i>Snipe Coenocorypha aucklandica </i> (GRAY, 1845) ... Snipe found on some of New Zealand's outer islands are named for their resemblance to the migratory Gallinago species of the northern hemisphere. <i>(1985,Reader's Digest Book of NZ Birds,202</i>)

>  <b>SCOTT</b> At that age he began standing in for his father ... hunting pigs and shooting snipe (godwits) on the dunes. <i>(1987,Seven Lives on Salt River,90</i>)

>  <b>ANDERSON</b> ... but no other sort of game was seen except a single snipe [ed. fn There is no native New Zealand snipe: this one must have been a migrant from Japan, <i>Gallinago hardwicki.</i>] which was shot and differs but little from that of Europe.] <i>(Feb 1777,Journal</i>) [NOTES: 1777 Feb Anderson's Journal in Cook Journals (1967) 3/807 (Queen Charlotte Sound)]

>  <b>CRUISE</b> At noon we went on the island to shoot, and killed some red bill and a snipe; the only one that any of us had seen in this country: in its plumage it resembled those found in England, but the bird itself was much smaller. <i>(1823,Journal,150,1957</i>) [NOTES: 1820 Aug 30 in 1823 Cruise Journal (1957) 150]

>  <b>WILLIAMS</b> ... we have had fresh baked bread, puddings ...ducks, snipe and pigeons; fish of various kinds ... <i>(Mar 28, 1833,Early Journals of Henry Williams, The,302,1961</i>)

>  <b>SARA MATHEW</b> We saw myriads of snipes [in North Auckland] in the shoal water and shot a dozen of these graceful birds. <i>(Apr 29, 1840,Journal</i>) [NOTES: 1840 Apr 29 Sarah Mathew Journal in 1940 Founding of NZ 132]

>  <i>Gallinago aucklandica </i>, Gray. Snipe. - Met with in the Chatham Island group. <i>(Nov 1885,NZ Journal of Science,85</i>) [NOTES: (T.H. Potts)]

>  <i>Gallinago aucklandica </i>. - Snipe. Auckland Islands. <i>(1886,TrNZI,18/113</i>) [NOTES: (Martin)]

>  Several interesting land birds inhabit the [Snares] island, ... the Auckland Island Snipe >Gallinago Aucklandica </i>); the grass bird (<i>Sphoeneacus fulvus </i>), although now rare on the mainland, was frequent on this little island ... <i>(1891,NZ Journal of Science,1/161</i>)

>  ... the most important [Chatham Island] edible sea-birds: AS WRITTEN AS PRONOUNCED ENGLISH hopo ho[macron]p' albatross hakoakoa ha[macron]ko[macron]k' mutton bird taiko tchai[macron]k' pied shear water tupoupou tchu[macron]poup' pied blue billie reoreo ro[macron]ro[macron] Mother Carys chicken turiwati tchu[macron]riwat' dottrel [sic] kuaka ku[macron]k' snipe <i>(1928,BP Bishop Memoirs,Vol. IX No. 5 p.358</i>) [NOTES: 1928 Baucke Manuscript in Skinner and Baucke The Morioris (Bishop Museum Memoirs Vol. IX No. 5 pp. 343-382) 358]

>  A COMPACT FARM, containing 43 acres of Land, situated at OREWA .. An Oyster bed within three minutes' walk, and plenty of Pigeon, Snipe, and Pheasant shooting. <i>(Dec 2, 1864,Daily Southern Cross,3</i>) [NOTES: Advert]

>  What takes B C down the Coast so often on Sundays? To shoot snipe I suppose. <i>(Dec 7, 1895,Observer (Auckland),21</i>)

>  A few plants common to the Auckland Isles, were also found in Fouveaux Strait, and one bird, a snipe, excited our curiosity as being the first of these species seen in New Zealand. <i>(Jul 24, 1852,New Zealand Spectator & Cook's Strait Guardian,3</i>)

>  THE other evening one of our sportsmen came home with a string of snipe. <i>(Sep 19, 1885,Waikato Times,6</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. sawmilling: to trim the end of a log to obviate snagging while snigging; sc a log ?variant of snip

>  If the weather is favourable, the log is `sniped' or rounded at one end, an iron grip driven into it, and to this the team is fastened. <i>(1902,NZ Illustrated Magazine,5/375</i>)

>  <b>R. GILBERD</b> A `ropey' will learn to `snipe' ... which is a highly-skilled operation. Butt-end of clean-trimmed log is trimmed of angles. Vees are cut at points opposite each other at the butt-end (usually) and are connected by a chopped Dee which runs around in a semi-circle from one to the other. In the Dee is laid a `strop', a short length of cable with an eye in each end. The eyes are connected with each other and to a short chain by a shackle; and the chain is attached to `the rope' with a hitch. <i>(1950,Personal Communication</i>)

>  <b>REED</b> In order to prevent the log from `biting' into uneven ground, and enable it to slip over minor obstacles, it was `sniped' - that is, somewhat rounded or tapered at the front. <i>(1953,Story of the Kauri, The,179</i>)

>   <i>(1958,NZ Timber Journal,87/2</i>) [NOTES: [ca -1914]]

>  After the logs were cut, each was sniped. To snipe a log, the end is chipped all the way round so that it can be handled without catching humps in the ground, stumps and so on; in fact you might say that a log when it is sniped looks rather like the blunt end of a whale. <i>(1951,Radio NZ / National Radio</i>) [NOTES: H.S. McCarroll The Days of the Kauri Bushmen [Radio Talk 2: TS]]

>  SNIPE To round off the end of a log in order to facilitate snigging. <i>(1952,NZ Forest Glossary</i>)

>  <b>MOORE</b> The front end of the log was carefully `sniped', that is, its sharp edge was rounded to allow it to skid like a sledge-runner. <i>(1969,From Forest to Farm,42</i>)

>  <b>OWEN & PERKINS</b> First of all they tapered one end, rounding the log so that it would be able to slide over impediments in its path, because it had to be dragged along the ground. Now these men were called `snipers', and having sniped the log, they then made two cuts, one on each side of the log opposite each other, right into the rounded part - the sniped end. That was for the purpose of holding a heavy chain which attached the log to the yoked bullocks ... <i>(1986,Speaking for Ourselves,159</i>) [NOTES: (Joe Gasparich, Northland kauri country)]

>  <b>BENNETT</b> A person complaining of another's ill-will might also say, `He's got a proper snitch on me' - obviously a variant of `to snitch upon' (to inform against) <i>(1943,English as it is spoken in NZ,90</i>)

>  <b>SLATTER</b> Got a snitch on me and put me in crook with the boss. <i>(1959,Gun in My Hand, A,91</i>)

>  But he wasn't a man to get a snitch on his neighbours because of a bit of bad luck ... <i>(1966,NZ Short Stories,128</i>) [NOTES: 1966 NZ Short Stories (1976) 128 (Middleton `Saving the Breed')]

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i> snitch on</> feeling of ill will; eg Gordon Slatter in <i>The Pagan Game </i>: `The selector had a snitch on me.' NZA. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,105</i>)</i>

### snitcher

 
<i>noun</i>. a dislike or grudge; a snitch q.v.

>  <b>SARGESON</b> It was Brixton's habit, this talking to himself, a long monologue which reproduced the slang of forty years ago. >  Sirs: Your `Housewife' has apparently taken a `snitcher' on us schoolteachers - largely, I suggest, over the anything but usual behaviour of one of us, but does she refuse to buy meat because one butcher gave her short weight? <i>(Apr 1953,Here & Now,35</i>) [NOTES: (G.Green)]

>  It was true that he had accused her of misconduct with another man. This was due to a story 'somebody had pitched into him'. He was perhaps silly for taking any notice of it, as the man might have had a 'snitcher' on him and was trying to 'put it across him'. <i>(Feb 4, 1926,NZ Truth,5</i>)

### snow comb

<i>noun</i>. a type of comb used in shearing machines

### snow-apple

 
<i>noun</i>.

[NOTES: Kolstad says these are species of <i>Gaultheria</i> and snow-apple in this sense does not appear to occur elsewhere, only in OED2 and US Dictionaries as an apple cultivar. Kerry Carman writes (Sep. 2000): I can supply no other literary reference to snow apples but am sure Neave was referring to the Alpine Snowberry <i>Gaultheria depressa</i> or, more likely, the closely-related <i>G.d.</i> var <i>novae-zelandiae</i> (Mountain Snowberry) with pure white apple-shaped fruits. These, at 1.5 cm, are the largest and juiciest berries in the genus.]

>  It is certain that snow-apple is a colloquial colonial term for the plant we now refer to as snowberry - possibly the Bush Snowberry <i>Gaultheria antipoda</i>, which is common on Mt Somers. But more likely, from Naeve's description of the fruit, is the Alpine Snowberry <i>Gaultheria depressa</i>, or the closely related <i>G d novaezelandiae</i>, the Mountain Snowberry, distinguished by its pure white, apple-shaped fruits, which, at 1.5 cm, are the largest, juiciest and generally regarded as tastiest in the genus. <i>(Dec 9, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),45</i>)

>  <b>ANDERSON</b> "We were up at 7.30 o'clock, took some sandwiches and started off to climb Mt Somers. Walked through bush and scrub and over stones, shifting shingle and boulders. Ate any amount of snow-apples, little white berries growing like cranberries and tasting like apples and cream". <i>(1965,Good Logs of Algidus, The,47</i>) [NOTES: Quote from Frank Naeve, written 1864]

### snowball waltz

 
<i>noun</i>. A means of breaking the ice; a pre-selected split up when the music stops and each takes a new partner from others in the hall; this continues until all are on the floor.

[NOTES: Also the name of a book by Renee. Note on conversation with Deidre Macken (60 yrs) about her mother's story (86 yrs). She was in the Wellington Ballet Company in 1926 and on news of Pavlova's tour wrote to her manager enquiring how they could help make her tour and reception more pleasant, her favourite colours, foods, etc. She expressed a great liking for meringue (cakes) so they consulted a chef who produced 3 attempts (e.g. a square cake was rejected in favour of a round one); finally the `soft-centre' variety was chosen. In her honour they named it Pavlova (?cake) and they presented this to Pavlova (? at a gathering) and she liked it a great deal. D. Macken is to research this - ? Ballet company records, etc. Deidre Macken (04) 384-6073 -  H.D. Macken, Nairn St.]

>  At its compulsive best, The Snowball Waltz is an acutely rendered portrayal of human frailty and unexpected fortitude. <i>(Dec 13, 1997,Listener (New Zealand Listener),46</i>)

>  With her latest novel, The Snowball Waltz, Renee has reached a new pinnacle of success... The novel takes its title from a dance which begins with two partners who, when the music stops, separate and seek new partners. <i>(Oct 26, 1997,Sunday Star Times,E6</i>)

[NOTES: Kerry Carman writes (Sept. 2000): <i>Gaultheria antipoda</i> is the Bush Snowberry; fruits are 15 mm and may be white, pink, red or purple. Confusing the issue are two other candidates, also commonly called snowberries. (a). <i>Pernettya</i> is also an edible Snowberry, sometimes white, sometimes red. Like <i>Gaultheria</i> it is of the <i>Ericaceae</i> with which it bydrisies freely in the wild. (b). <i>Leucopogon (Epacridaceae)</i> is another edible native Snowberry from the region. It ranges from white through pinks and red to purple.]

>  <b>CROWE</b> Snowberry <i>Gaultheria antipoda</i> Tawiniwini; bush snowberry <i>Gaultheria depressa</i> Mountain snowberry... >  <b>BROOKER et al.</b> <i>Gaultheria antipoda</i> Forst.f. Common name: <i>Snowberry </i>Maori name: <i>Papapa </i>... This little shrub is common throughout New Zealand in scrubland. Possibly it is the plant referred to by James Cowan [in Maori Today] ... although Williams identifies `papapa' as both <i>Pomaderris elliptica</i> (Rhamnaceae) and <i>Gaultheria antipoda</i>. <i>(1981,NZ Medicinal Plants,52</i>)

>  <b>McLINTOCK</b> Snowberry .. .. taupuka, taupuku .. .. <i>Gaultheria</i> <i>(1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,3/705-712</i>)

>  <b>HALL-JONES</b> ... called the New Zealand strawberry [more commonly called the snowberry or Gaultheria depressa] ... <i>(1971,Mr Surveyor Thomson,61</i>)

>  All over the spurs and ridges the snowberry (<i>Gaultheria antipoda</i>) was found plentifully, and picked and eaten largely by the party, its delicious coolness being enhanced by the heat of the day. <i>(Feb 17, 1872,Otago Witness,14</i>)

>  Typical of the sites he surveyed was Macraes Flat, where, in 1986, he noted that porcupine shrubs, snowberry plants and pohuehue vines were stripped of all their ripe fruit where they grew on outcrops inhabited by grand skinks, while plants on nearby outcrops without skinks were untouched. <i>(Jul 2000,NZ Geographic,No. 47/70</i>)

>  It certainly makes for more interesting walks, when.. you can recognise such delights as ceps, snowberries, or cape gooseberries. <i>(Mar 13, 1993,Otago Daily Times,11</i>)

>  <b>CAVE & PADDISON</b> Gaultheria. Ericaceae. A genus of 120 species of shrubby plants found mainly in the Americas. There are about 10 New Zealand species, of which all but 1 are endemic. Their common name is snowberry because they bear white to pinkish red fruit. <i>(1999,Gardener's Encyclopedia of New Zealand Plants, The,211</i>)

>  <b>RILEY</b> The pink, red or white berries of this shrub were gathered in the past by men of the village when larger, more tasty berries were unobtainable. Snowberries are a favourite food of the weka bird, they were also sought by the early sheep musterers and prospectors of Otago in the high country when emergency rations were needed. <i>(1994,Maori Healing & Herbal,322</i>)

>  <b>WILSON</b> Gaultheria sp. Snowberry... after Gaulthier, French Canadian. <i>(1982,Stewart Island Plants,114</i>)

>  <b>METCALFE</b> Snowberries are quite edible, although the taste is perhaps somewhat over-rated. In earlier years country people, especially in Otago and Southland, used to gather the fruits and make snowberry pies. <i>(1993,Cultivation of NZ Plants, The,144</i>)

>  <b>MALCOM, B. & N.</b> Sometimes plants belonging to even different genera can cross - for example, our native <i>Gaultheria</i>, and <i>Pernettya</i> snow-berries cross shamelessly, and only expert field botanists and biochemists can figure out which of the several species in the genus are the parents of the hybrid. <i>(1988,New Zealand's Alpine Plants Inside & Out,105</i>)

>  <b>SALMON</b> Snowberries belonging to the genera <i>Gaultheria</i> and <i>Pernettya</i>are found throughout the New Zealand mountains from subalpinbe scrub to the higher herb and fellfields. All species have edible fruits, and records exist of people who have been sustained by eating them. <i>(1992,Alpine Plants of New Zealand (Field Guide),78</i>) [NOTES: 3rd ed. (1st ed. 1968)]

>  <b>DAWSON</b> <i>Gaultheria depressa</i> var. <i>novae-zelandiae</i> is a prostrate shrub in open places remarkable for its relatively large white, pink or red, berry-like fruits often referred to as 'snow berries'. <i>(1998,Forest Vines to Snow Tussocks,168</i>)

>  <b>COCKAYNE</b> The Heath Family (Ericaceae) is represented only by the snowberries (<i>Gaultheria</i> and <i>Pernettya</i>). <i>(1967,NZ Plants & Their Story,220</i>) [NOTES: 4th edition]

>  <b>LAING & BLACKWELL</b> The white fruit of <i>G. antipoda</i> is known as the snowberry in Otago, and is occasionally eaten. Like most of the products of the New Zealand bush, it cannot be recommended to the epicure. <i>(1949,Plants of NZ,344</i>) [NOTES: 5th edition]

>  <b>THOMSON</b> Masses of flax and speargrass, intermingled with tussac, matagori scrub, snowberry and anise, covered the open ground, and among these grew a profusion of smaller heaths and nerteras, yielding abundant food for birds. <i>Ibid.</i> 212 Kakas were abundant in those days both in the bush and in the open, where they dug at the roots of the speargrass and flax for the larger grubs to be found there, or visited the flax flowers for nectar and the snowberry and ground tutu for their fruit. <i>(1909,NZ Naturalist's Calendar,211</i>)

>  <b>CROWE</b> Richards describes the fruit of the creeping mountain snowberry as 'edible and rather tasteless.' Earlier travellers, who had perhaps worked up a better appetite, have kinder words for them; J.T. Thomson, while exploring South Otago in 1857, seemed to appreciate the New Zealand strawberry, as he called it, and likens it to the rose apple of India. <i>(1990,Native Edible Plants of NZ,54</i>) [NOTES: 1st ed. 1981]

>  <b>TAYLOR</b> I was so weak that I thought I must give in, but I ate plenty of the little snow-berries which grow under the snow. They helped us on a good deal, and we reached the top about 2 p.m. [Fn: <i>Gaultheria depressa</i>. <i>(1959,Early Travellers,413</i>)

>  <b>CROWE</b> I find the flavour of raw snowberries generally sweet and juicy, though later in the season they can be rather dry and tasteless. <i>(1990,Native Edible Plants of NZ,54</i>)

>  Snowberries (<i>Gaultheria</i> spp) are the most familiar alpine berries, coming in a succulent [47] red, pink or white. <i>Ibid.</i> Snowberry, <i>Gaultheria colensoi</i>, a member of the heath family, is a sprawling, small-leafed shrub found only in the central North Island and Ruahine Ranges. <i>(Sep 2001,NZ Geographic,No. 53/44</i>)

>  <b>WAITT</b> My great delight was to gather the New Zealand snowberry. This little pure white berry ... the fruit pure as the snow, the leaf and plant like a Scotch blacberry.[sic] <i>(1856,Letter,10</i>) [NOTES: 1856 Waitt Letter to Joseph Thomas 10]

>  I ate plenty of little snow-berries which grow under the snow. <i>(Jul 2, 1864,Lake Wakatip Mail</i>) [NOTES: 1864 July 2-16 Lake Wakatip Mail (Alphonse Barrington) in Knox Thousand Mountains Shining 202]

>  <b>BARRINGTON</b> I was so weak that I thought I must give in, but I ate plenty of the little snow-berries which grow under [414] the snow. ... [fn]<i>Gaultheria depressa</i> <i>(May 17, 1864,Diary,413</i>)

>  <b>MURPHY</b> <i>Gaultheria antipoda </i>snowberry <i>(1885,Handbook of NZ Gardening</i>) [NOTES: (And)]

>  <b>HETLEY</b> <i>Gaultheria antipoda </i>snowb erry <i>(1888,Native Flowers of NZ</i>) [NOTES: (And)]

>  <b>MATTHEWS</b> <i>Gaultheria rupestris</i> snowberry <i>(1890,Descriptive & Priced List</i>) [NOTES: (And)]

>  <b>COCKAYNE</b> <i>Gaultheria antipoda</i> snowberry <i>(1919,NZ Plants & Their Story</i>) [NOTES: (And)]

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> The snowberries were fine. We called the red hill kind [c1840] `mulberries', but I do not know why. <i>Ibid.</i>122-123 Berries were conspicuous by their absence as [123] a general rule, but the snowberries flourished in some parts, ... <i>(1939,First White Boy Born in Otago,18</i>)

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> On the tussocky sides of gullies the pleasant-tasting snowberries grew in profusion, while a berry known as the wind-berry grew on a little plant similar to the snowberries and both kinds were eaten and enjoyed. <i>(1947,Pioneer Recollections,5,1965</i>)

### snowdropper

### snowed in

 
<i>noun</i>. of the condition when shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table

>  <b>BOWEN</b> SNOWED IN. Describing the state of affairs when the shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table. With a good run shearers can sometimes snow the pressers in. Shearers will be seen at their best when they get ahead of the rest of the shed. They enjoy this snowing in, and usually they make the wool flow faster than ever. <i>(1956,Wool Away!,157</i>) [NOTES: (glossary: Shearing Terms)]

>  <i>Snowed in</i>: The condition of the sorting table or the shearing board when shearers are working too fast for the shed hands to keep up. <i>(Feb 26, 1965,Listener (New Zealand Listener)</i>) [NOTES: (H.A.L. Laing)]

>  SNOWED IN: The condition of the table or board when the shearers are working too fast for the shed hands to keep up. <i>(Feb 21, 1968,Straight Furrow,20</i>) [NOTES: [Shearer's language]]

>  <i>Snowed in</i>: When shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table. Also described as woolled-up. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,59</i>)

>  <i>snowed in</i>: When the shearers get ahead of the men on the wool table and fleeces lie around. <i>(1989,NZ English Newsletter,3/28</i>) [NOTES: (Wallace Shearing Glossary)]



 
<i>adjective</i>. [Rural] [of a woolshed floor] filled with unrolled fleeces when shearers' work is ahead of shed-hands'.

>  <b>BOWEN</b> Snowed in. Describing the state of affairs when the shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table. <i>(1955,Wool Away!,157</i>)

>  <b>MAF</b> Snowed-in: when shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,58</i>)

>  <b>SQUIRE</b> Snowed in: (woolled up) The condition of the table or the board when shearers are working too fast for shed hands to keep up. [snowed in] <i>(1991,A to Z Glossary of Wool Terms,49</i>)

### snowed off, be

 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to encounter serious snowy conditions that prevent mustering.

<i>verb</i>.

<i>noun</i>.

### snowgrass

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  There are many less conspicuous snow grasses whose flags don't catch our eye so well. <i>(Aug 27, 1999,Dominion,14</i>)

>  Pale-green snowgrass and red tussock appear as we pull ourselves up to the peaks of Matanginui and then Maharahara at 1100m. <i>(Dec 20, 2003,Dominion Post,E8</i>)

>  We followed the saddle towards Balloon over snow grass and most agreeable travel. <i>(Feb 27, 1890,Otago Witness,34</i>)

>  Stiffer soils.. such as those which produce the large coarse tussock popularly called snow grass, are not good producers of the clovers. <i>(Oct 30, 1890,Otago Witness,17</i>)

>  There we were, stuck for the night and no more shelter than a snow-grass tussock over us. <i>(Nov 11, 1897,Otago Witness,60</i>)

>  <i>Snow </i> (sn&omacr.)<i>, n. [Add.] Snow grass. (Bot.) (a)</i> A coarse, tall grass of New Zealand (<i>Danthonia Raouli </i>), persistent through the water. (b) Tussock grass (<i>Poa caespitosa </i>). <i>(1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [high country] a tall-growing tussock of Danthonia spp., that can be grazed by sheep when other feed is unavailable.

>  Cutting snowgrass for thatch. <i>(May 3, 1867,Castle Station Diary</i>) [NOTES: in VANCE (1965) High Endeavour 257]

>  <b>STUDHOLME</b> The Maori track which led through it to the lake had numerous turns and twists in it to avoid the clumps of snowgrass, manuka and cabbage-trees. <i>(1940,Te Waimate,67</i>)

>  <b>CONNELL & HADFIELD</b> By a dominant plant is meant that plant in a community which gives the community its characteristic appearance and which may control its structure, e.g. beech in South Island bush, kauri in North Auckland bush, and snow grass in the grassland of the high country in the South Island. <i>(1961,Agriculture,292</i>)

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> snowgrass: big straggly tussocks standing up to four feet high or more and of even greater diameter. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,74</i>)

>  <b>STACEY</b> With everyone in position we were running through soaking snowgrass trying to muster off as soon as possible. <i>(1996,Tales of a Tussock Jumper,57</i>)

>  <b>CURTIS</b> There was a 200 metre band of snowgrass which ran for about two kilometres, in places extending down between scrubby ridges to reach almost the valley floor. <i>(1996,Beneath the Mountain Mist,57</i>)

### snowgrass country

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] high-country land that grows tussock and can only be grazed in summer.

>  <b>NEWTON</b> The ridge .. runs to little over 5,000 feet and as it is all open snowgrass country, it is inevitable that the two stations have an annual exchange of stragglers. <i>(1952,High Country Journey,156</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> Mainly over 3,000 feet, it is primarily red tussock, or snowgrass country, much of it still in its original state. <i>(1969,Big Country of the North Island,139</i>)

>  <b>MCCASKILL</b> The high-altitude snowgrass country above 4,000 feet occupied about 2,000 acres. <i>(1973,Hold This Land,88</i>)

>  We came out in the snow-grass country. <i>(Sep 30, 1924,Otago Witness,67</i>)

### snowline

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a high country area above which sheep are not grazed in safety except in mid-summer.

>  <b>ANDERSON</b> In winter the high tops remain permamently snowbound down to a line of about 900 metres; hence the ward `snowline' <i>(1981,Both Sides of the River,8</i>)

>  <b>ANDERSON</b> A greater number of stations have snowline fences on their winter blocks, ... <i>(1981,Both Sides of the River,8</i>)

>  <b>CHARLES</b> There's no place I'd rather be,/ Than the top beat/ With a snow-line boundary./ <i>(1981,Black Billy Tea,35</i>)

>  <i> Snowline</i>.-A correspondent writes: your usage is, of course, different from that of mountaineers, who speak of it as the lower limit of permanent snow in summer.' <i>(Jan 27, 1934,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland]

>  Mountain peaks and ridges above the snowline. <i>(1915,NZ Geol. Survey Bulletin,No6 (N.S.)/11</i>) [NOTES: (Morgan) The Geology.. of the Buller-Mokihinui  Subdivision.Westland]

>  The grassy downs, the hills from base to snow line clad with various verdure, seem to invite the lowing herds and bleating flocks; ... <i>(Dec 4, 1858,Otago Witness</i>) [NOTES: 1858 Dec 4 Otago Witness in 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 9]

>  <b>BUTLER</b> Here and there at the mouths of the rivers a few flats may exist or rather do exist, but over these rolls upward to the snow line a heaving mass of timber. <i>(Jun 1860,Forest Creek MS,54,1960</i>)

>  <b>A TRAMP</b> The land ... extends from the snow-line right up to the sleeted peaks <i>(1891,Casual Ramblings,53</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> <i>Snow-line, n.</i> In pastoralists' language of New Zealand, `above the snow-line' is land covered by snow in winter, but free in summer. <i>(1898,Austral English,425</i>)

>  <b>PASCOE</b> At one time the Kakapo screamed in the birch country from the sea beach to near the snow line <i>(1957,Mr Explorer Douglas,259</i>) [NOTES: (Birds SW.) c 1899]

>  The merino occupies and thrives on the wild lands of the colony, from the snow-line to the border of the plains, ... <i>(1902,Settler's Handbook of NZ, The,92</i>)

>  <i>Snow line</i>.- Roughly the line above which snow lies all the winter and therefore the country above the <i>s.l.</i> is only useful for sheep from October (or even after shearing) until May. <i>(Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  The glaciers, in some instances, appear to be considerably lower than the snowline: on the shaded side of Mount Alta, a little below the summit, there is one about five acres in extent, and three feet in thickness. <i>(Jul 26, 1862,Otago Witness,3</i>)

>  Had it been left to the Motueka public a good track would have been laid out before the snow came to prevent it, and long ere this the track for horses would have been completed up to the snowline, and then finished when the snow cleared off, thus half the work would have been done. <i>(Oct 1, 1870,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,4</i>)

>  A glacier which has been in descent since first discovered has now nearly reached the timber-line, and we were treated to the singular sight of a large body of ice in midsummer nearly 4000 feet below the snowline. <i>(Mar 4, 1882,Otago Witness,12</i>)

>  The snowline is very near to the road just here, and the piercing wind of a morning would not give second place even to the "barber" at the Grey. <i>(Jun 23, 1913,Grey River Argus,4</i>)

>  <b>HENDERSON</b> By the snowline, just above the scrubline, all of a sudden, especially early December, there was a vast sea of mountain flowers ahead. <i>(1984,Tales of the Coast,33</i>)

>  <b>GORDON</b> Retiring back valleys and land above the snowline (900m or 3,000 ft) is part of a soil conservation scheme to protect mountain lands. <i>(1987,People, Places & Paddocks,179</i>)

>  <i>~ n.-</i>snow'-line n. in New Zealand, the elevation on the mountains which snow is found in winter but not in the summer. <i>(1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,2031</i>)

### snowman

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>MACDONALD</b> All freezing was done for the first ten years [from c1882] by the cold air machines ...[66] The carcases were hung in the chambers, and the cold air was blown through kauri ducts or trunks at a temperature of minus 40[degree sign] Fahrenheit. The carcases, being relatively warmer than the air, always lost moisture to it; this formed snow which blocked the trunks, cutting down the air circulation and giving the `snow-men', who had to crawl through the trunks, a bad time in clearing them. <i>(1957,Canterbury Frozen Meat Company,65</i>)

>  <b>SIMPSON</b> An expression in common use Down Under is soap the geyser. A crazy one, surely. It is confined almost exclusively to New Zealand, and its origin is no mystery ... In the Thermal Regions of New Zealand there is a particular geyser that could be made to perform by throwing soap into it, and it was frequently soaped so that it would put up a display for the delight of important visitors. So today, when a New Zealander says, `Come on, let's soap the geyser', he means `Come on, let's get going', or `Let's start' <i>(1945,If You'd Care to Know,100</i>)

### soldier settler

Yes, actually sitting in judgement on him! These names have a bearing on some distinguishing characteristic of the fish. ... The name Soldierfish is derived from the similarities of this fish to the activities of a soldier or picket on sentinel duty. ### solstice

 
<i>noun</i>.

[NOTES: Jim writes: As an attributive, in relation to the winter solstice, this has come into use in NZ recently in compounds such as <i>(winter) solstice carnival, solstice celebration, solstice dinner, solstice party</i>. Any similar usages in the Northern Hemisphere (none are recorded in NSOD or Collins) are likely to relate to the summer solstice, since the winter solstice coincides with Christmas. I havs also seen <i>winter Christmas</i> used in NZ. The development of "solstice" terms might usefully be watched.]

>  <b>SUTHERLAND</b> Although inadvertently administered, Angus had been under the influence of `sool,' which gave him an unfair advantage over an enemy who was, for the moment, peaceably inclined. Officialdom does things the hard way. `It is to be forbidden,' says the Institute, `in any public place, to set on, urge, encourage, aid or assist any dog to rush at, attack or worry any person or animal.' This would seem to include baiting, egging, sooling and/or sic-ing, though not specifically mentioned. <i>(1953,Golden Bush, The,122,1963</i>)

>  <b>SLATTER</b> The crowd swaying on the terraces, ... the crowd sooling the teams on for blood. <i>(1968,Pagan Game, The,175</i>)

>  <b>MARKS</b> Gee whiz! How Bill did sool him! <i>(1934,Memories (Mainly Merry),60</i>)

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>sool</i> set a dog on somebody; from `sowl', English dialect word meaning to handle roughly; eg `If you jokers don't clear off I'll sool the dog on ya.' NZA. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,106</i>)

>  A SCOLDING WOMAN.- The barbarities of the ducking stool for the cure of scolding women, though abolished by law, are now sometimes practiced [sic] by a kind of social barbarity none the less reprehensible. The nerves will be quieted, and acerbity of word and thought will give place to amiability and affection. Healthy women do not scold ... <i>(Dec 29, 1886,Wanganui Herald,2</i>) [NOTES: nb wrongly placed, word at the end is blurred on original but is scold, not sool.  Advert]

>  'He wants to snavel our land.. sool'im an' snavel HIS land!" <i>(Oct 1919,Quick March,33</i>)

>  We would suggest that some practical usemight be made of those "beautiful womenspies" if they were sooled on to theinner ring of the profiteering business. <i>(Dec 16, 1919,Evening Post</i>)

### sooner

>  <b>GASCOIGNE</b> Manu was sitting on the top rail of the sorting pens in the shade of a willow tree. <i>(1965,From the Top of a Hill,26</i>)

>  <b>GASCOIGNE</b> Manu would drive about one hundred in to the crown pen which supplied the narrow sorting pens where we worked under a roof. <i>(1965,From the Top of a Hill,68</i>)

### sorting shed

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a shed in which wool is sorted during scouring and pressing.

>  The woolpacks which come down from the country loosely packed and very imperfectly pressed, are received into the sorting shed, which is fitted up for the accomodation of eleven sorters. <i>(Jan 2, 1869,Otago Witness,15</i>)

>  <b>BREMNER</b> In the late 1930s expansion continued. A Model AA Ford truck took wool out to the paddock, and a third sorting shed was built. <i>(1985,Woolscours of NZ,65</i>)

>  <b>BREMNER</b> The new sorting shed of 1924 is the high roof at the rear .. a store for greasy wool which was hoisted to the sorting shed. <i>(1985,Woolscours of NZ,70</i>)

### sorting table

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a wool table in a woolshed, where fleeces are trimmed, sorted and rolled.

>  Boys are employed to remove the fleeces as quickly as they are shorn, and to take them to the sorting table. <i>(Feb 23, 1876,Tuapeka Times,2</i>)

>  FARMERS wishing to shear their Sheep at the Ashburton or Tinwald Saleyards will find every convenience provided, including Woolpress, Sorting Table, &c. <i>(Oct 12, 1887,Ashburton Guardian,3</i>)

>  Work begins usually at five a.m. to the click of the shears; the fleeces are taken off deftly by the practised hands who can easily do their hundred a day, and carried to the sorting table. <i>(Apr 1, 1907,Progress,213</i>)

>  The wool is carried to the sorting table, and placed by the sorter in its several bins, from whence it is removed by the pressers, who by the aid of a powerful screw press turn it out in firm compact bales. <i>(Feb 6, 1869,Otago Witness,6</i>)

>  1 Sorting Table and Trestles and Sundries. <i>(Oct 14, 1898,Timaru Herald,3</i>) [NOTES: Advert]

>  <b>BATHGATE</b> Meanwhile the 'pickers up' were busy .. and carrying them to the sorting table, where they were stripped of the 'pieces' ... <i>(1881,Waitaruna,172</i>)

>  <b>FERNANDEZ</b> Erina, as usual, had been giving him saucy looks and cheek over the sorting table ... <i>(1973,Tussock Fever,72</i>)

>  THE N.Z. FARMERS' CO-OPERATIVE DISTRIBUTING CO., LTD., have been favoured with instructions from Mr. T. Riddler, who is giving up business, to sell by public auction, WITHOUT RESERVE, the whole of his plant, comprising .. 2 Sorting Tables ... <i>(Jun 8, 1914,Evening Post,10</i>)

>  Motor lorries can, and do, pull right into the shed of the way-back small farmer and load his wool right from the sorting tables. <i>(Dec 6, 1928,NZ Truth,6</i>)

### sound

 
<i>verb</i>.

<i>adjective</i>. [Rural] [of stock, stock anatomy, farm materials, wool, pasture, crops, machines, houses, seasons, shelter belts, fences etc] reliable or healthy.

>  Subdivided into 22 main paddocks, the farm has a high-quality gravel, all weather laneway and sound shelter belts. <i>(Apr 12, 2001,NZ Farmer,39</i>)

>  Clean and cattle-safe medium/steep hill country with sound fencing and fertiliser history. <i>(May 31, 2002,Dominion Post,17</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a fiord

>   <i>(1885,TrNZI,17/187</i>) [NOTES: (A. Reischek)]

### sound-mouthed

 
<i>adjective</i>. [Rural] [of sheep] with numerous healthy teeth.

>  full-mouthed ewes 13s 10d .. 232 sound-mouthed at 13s 8d. <i>(Feb 3, 1906,Farmers' Union Advocate,7</i>)

>  Stock Report: Sound-mouthed ewes $18 to $19. <i>(Mar 6, 1991,NZ Farmer,37</i>)

### soundness

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a quality or grade of fleece wool

>  soundness - this means that the fibres of the wool are strong and the staple free from any break. <i>(Jul 1892,NZ Farmer,291</i>)

>  <b>BARTON</b> Thus it seems that the factors contributing to fibre length (staple length, soundness and freedom from cotting) could be of greater future importance. <i>(1971,Sheepfarming Annual 1971,5</i>)

>  <b>BARTON</b> Apart from the comments Good to Super wools should be 'free from break' and other grades 'slightly webby or tender' no references have been made to soundness ... <i>(1972,Sheepfarming Annual 1972,114</i>)

>  <b>MAF</b> Sound: wool without a tensile weakness. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,59</i>)

>  <b>SQUIRES</b> Soundness - the tensile strength of the staple. A laboratory test can measure breaking force in 'Newtons per kilotex' and position of break along the staple. <i>(1991,A to Z Glossary of Wool Terms,36</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a qualitative state of breeding stock.

>  40 years of free calving on Hill Country where cow performance and soundness are of paramount importance. <i>(May 31, 2002,Dominion Post,22</i>)

>  Bull Sale ... 3 year guarantee for soundness & fertility. <i>(Jun 6, 2002,Taranaki Daily News,21</i>)

### South Island kokako

 
<i>noun</i>. [Environment]

>  The South Island kokako is said to have been extinct for the past 30 years, although "missing in action" may be a better description as there have been plenty of tantalising clues to suggest that the bird still exists... the South Island kokako is, or was, about the size of a magpie, with steel-grey plumage and distinctive coloured wattles at the base of its beak. It is a distinct subspecies from its North Island neighbour, which has blue wattles and had avoided extinction thanks to a determined effort by the Department of Conservation. ### southerly buster

 
<i>noun</i>. ? orig Canterbury, but general South Island and Cook Strait. see esp. buster, and see butt=ender; see also south-easter, souther, southern buster, sou'west buster, threeday sou'wester Acland's note and description (1933) applies (also CR. 68): A strong wind with rain, snow or sleet from a southerly direction. The ordinary man in the paddock in Canterbury recognises only three winds: <i> East </i> (from N.E.),<i> sou'wester </i> (from S.E., S. etc, S.W. etc), and nor'wester. <i> As a matter of fact a three-day so'wester usually only lasts two and a half. They are said to be less fierce than in the early days, just as the nor'wester is said to have been softened by the planting on the plains. It may be so in Christchurch </i>; but I cannot say I notice any difference up-country. The <i> nor'</i> wester <i> may come from any where between due north and due west. In such places as Hororata, where the wind can get at you between two gorges a distinction is made between a Waimakariri and a Rakaia nor' wester; but both are called nor' westers. </i>

[NOTES: Empty but for the note under definition]



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a cold wind from the south, usually bringing stormy rain, sleet and snow.

[NOTES: also southerly burster, rarely southern burster]

>  southerly buster n. a violent and sudden squall from the south. [corrupt. fr. buster] <i>(1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,3</i>)

>  <i>southerly buster </i>... An old name for a fierce storm from a southerly direction in both Australia and New Zealand. <i>(1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),55</i>)

>  <i>buster, southerly n.</i> sudden and violent squall from South particularly in Sydney [orig.<i> burster</i>]. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),5</i>)

>  Reference had been made to "southerly busters" as being the most dangerous winds as far as navigation in Cook Strait was concerned. <i>(Feb 18, 1921,Evening Post,7</i>)

>  The order of the day has been for some time past rain; rainbows and southerly bursters, yet there has been nothing but what might have been expected in the midst of winter thus far south, and especially as Port Cooper is the channel for South winds over the Isthmus of Banks Peninsula. <i>(Jul 4, 1851,Australian & NZ Gazette,30/483</i>) [NOTES: (Christchurch)]

>  <b>TANCRED</b> The suddenness of these [south-west] storms is expressed by the colonial name of `Southerly Bursters' <i>(1856,Natural History of Canterbury,26</i>)

>  <b>HURSTHOUSE</b> The greatest drawback of the [Canterbury] Plains is the want of shelter in the strong gales, `Southerly Bursters', which occasionally occur. <i>(1857,New Zealand (various authors/titles),2/372</i>)

>  <b>BUTLER</b> It is curious to watch the battle between the north-west and south-east wind, as we often see it. ... The southerly `burster', as it is called, gradually creeps up, and at last drives the other off the field. A few chilly puffs, then a great one, and in a minute or two the air becomes cold, even in the height of summer. <i>(1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,8/123</i>)

>  Southerly burster, - buster.- <i> Three-day Sou'Wester.</i> A strong wind with rain, snow or sleet from a southerly direction. The ordinary man in the paddock in Canterbury recognises only three winds: east (from NE), sou'-wester (from SE, S etc, SW, etc.) and nor'-wester. As a matter of fact a <i> t.d.sw </i>.' usually only lasts two and a half. They are said to be less fierce than in the early days, just as the <i> nw.</i> is said to have been softened by the planting on the plains. It may be so in Christchurch but I cannot say I notice any difference up country. The <i> nw </i>. may come from any where between due north and due west. In such places as Hororata, where the wind can get at you down two gorges, a distinction is made between a Waimakariri and a Rakaia <i> nw;</i> but both are called <i> nws </i>. `Where six-days a week the gale/ Laden thick with rain or [hail] First from sou'-west blows a piercer/ Then veers nor'-west and blows fiercer.' (C.RH., p. 68.) <i>(Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

### Southern Alps

 
<i>noun</i>. the main range of the South Island

>  It was for a long time believed that a practicable inland communication between the northern end of this island and the country to the southward did not exist, and that the rugged Kaikoras [sic] formed a barrier from the sea on the east coast, to the great chain of Southern Alps which crown the west coast of the island from its northern to its southernmost end. <i>(Jun 5, 1852,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,58</i>)

>  The Southern Alps in the Middle Island, form such a prominent feature in the landscape, that even the uncsientific traveller, when he passes along the west coast, cannot but admire their wild and fantastic forms, clad in a garment of snow, and standing boldly against the deep blue sky of New Zealand. <i>(Nov 6, 1861,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,4</i>)

>  Resuming our journey we came into view of Mount Aspiring, the Matterhorn of the Southern Alps, with its miles of snow and ice-fields glistening in the sunlight, and a little further on lay Pembroke and Lake Wanaka. <i>(Feb 1, 1900,NZ Illustrated Magazine,27</i>)

>  The foregoing is the title of an exhaustive paper written by Dr Teichelmann, which appears in the New Zealand Graphic Christmas number, with numerous illustrations from photographs taken by the Doctor on his annual mountaineering trips. The author's purpose is chiefly to show that the approach to the Southern Alps from the West Coast side is through more interesting country than from the Eastern side, and that the route is most accessible. <i>(Oct 20, 1904,West Coast Times,2</i>)

>  At last we landed on a rather muddy and very steep bank, and I almost forgot, in my eagerness to gain a firm footing, that I was indeed on Mount Cook, the monarch of the Southern Alps. <i>(Dec 23, 1890,Otago Witness,37</i>)

>  THE ARTHUR'S PASS TUNNEL. SOME PARTICULARS.This great work, of which all New Zealanders are justly proud, is to penetrate the Southern Alps under the 'Arthur's Pass Coach Road." [sic] <i>(Jan 20, 1910,Grey River Argus,1</i>)

>  THE MANAPOURI ALPSCATHEDRAL RANGE ASCENDED..[The Cathedral Peaks are a range on the northern side of Lake Manapouri, and although they are not so lofty as the main chain of the Southern Alps, their exceedingly precipitous character makes them so formidable to the tourist that an ascent has very seldom been attempted ...] <i>(Jan 9, 1915,Ashburton Guardian,2</i>)

>  IT is not everyone who is privileged to have some portion of the country named after him, but such has been the reward of Arthur Dudley Dobson, civil engineer and pioneer, of Canterbury, after whom Arthur's Pass was named. Mr. Dobson was the first man to traverse the narrow by-pass which gives access from the Canterbury Plains to the narrow productive strip of Westland lying to the west of the Southern Alps. <i>(May 9, 1929,NZ Truth,6</i>)

### Southern Alps gecko

 
<i>noun</i>. abundant in inland South Island, mottled grey brown gecko.

The Southern Alps gecko (,i>Hoplodactylus aff. maculatus 'Southern Alps'</i>) lives near rocky outcrops, screes, boulder banks and rock tumbles. The jewelled gecko (<i>Naultinus gemmeus</i>) lives in forest and shrubland. <i>(2009,Internet - see Notes</i>) [NOTES: http://doc.org.nz/publications/getting-involved/students-and-teachers/themes/river-life/lizards/]

In addition, the markings tend to be verydrab, and often include pinkish tones. <i>(Jan 2006,Internet - see Notes</i>) [NOTES: http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/otagogeckosa.pdf]

(c) Other common names: (i) Skipjack; Striped Bonito (ii) Bluefin Tuna; Southern Bluefin; Southern Tuna (iii) Yellowfin All sometimes referred to as Tunny. ### southern Buller's albatross

 
<i>noun</i>. [Environment] <i>Thalassarche bulleri</i>, Buller's albatross

See: Buller's albatross

>  In keeping with their commanding presence on the wing, on land southern Buller's albatrosses possess an aristocratic mien. Like several other species small albatross (also known as mollymawks) they have dark shadows under their brows, a crescent of dazzling white feathers behind the eyes, subtle shadings of grey over the head and neck and bright slabs of yellow in the bill. The southern Buller's albatross, <i>Thalassarche bulleri</i>, breeds only on the Snares and Solander Island, off the south Fiordland coast, while a closely related species, the northern Buller's albatross, has its breeding headquarters on the Chatham Islands. <i>(Jan 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 61/23</i>)

### Southern Hemisphere

 
<i>noun</i>. Constr comp or superl aj + (...) in the southern hemisphere: as an expression of inflated parochial comparison, much used in NZ (and in Australia) to give a false impression of comparative size etc.

<i>noun</i>.

### span-'em

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> In the nineteenth century the ring game seems to have been the most popular marble game. (In more recent years marble games with holes have had the greater role.) There was Big Ring, in which a circle a yard or more in diameter was drawn on the ground; there was the mullibar variation, in which an outsize taw was catapulted amongst the marbles in this circle. There were Little Ring, Liney, Follows, Follow the Taw, Holey, and then, on a less important scale, Butcher's Board, in which the marbles were bowled through the holes in a board, Eye-Drop, Knock-Backs, Leggings-Out (or Leggin's-Out), Span-'Em, and Backits. The last was more usually a girls' game. <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,174</i>)

### spang-weazling

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  Perhaps the most intriguing game of this nature [sc. tormenting insects or animals] is `Spang Weazling'. This game was played at Denniston in 1930-35. A crawley was placed on the end of a stick the middle section of which lay balanced over a stone. Before the crawley could crawl off the stick a stone had to be thrown onto the other end of the stick so as to catapult the crawley off the stick and over the cliff. A variation of the same game was being played at Denniston when I visited there in 1949. It was called alternatively `Hit the Crawley' or `Strike the Crayfish'. In this version the other end of the stick was hit with a batting stick (as in Tip Cat) and when the crawley was catapulted into the air it was hit again with the bat. <i>(1953,Unorganized Games,1/406</i>)

>  Some years ago there was a game among boys [?in Dunedin] called `spangweaselling' - taking kingfishers' nests with the young birds in them and knocking them to bits in the air. <i>(Aug 2, 1965,TV1</i>) [NOTES: 1965 Aug 2 WNTV1 `Any Questions' (P. Smithell, Dunedin) [spg SPANGWEASELING]]

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> <i>Spang-Weazling</i> (K-9) was a rather odd hitting game and appeared in only one locality, namely, Denniston, a mining village on the West Coast. [1920] <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,161</i>)

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> There are games recorded in this period for which there is no record before 1900 though they may well have existed under other names. est Coast: Dunk and Davey, Spang Weazling; <i>Wellington:</i> Who Goes Round My Stone Wall, Beg o' My Neighbor, Bellahonie, Run a Mile, On and Off the Bridge, Here Come Two Nuns, Colours, Isaac and Rebecca. Scrag, Diabolo, Bumble Puppy, Homai, Fives; <i>Auckland</i>: My Fair Young Lady, Rushes and Reeds, Surrender the Tower, Walls, Ball Hopscotch, ball games, Solomon Says; <i>Hawkes Bay</i>: Wolf Wolf Go Home, Homai; <i>Canterbury</i>: Poor Old Tom, Rats and Rabbits and Rips, Steps, Skin the Snake, Steal a Peg, Toodle-em-Buck, The Gag; <i>Golden Bay</i>: Who's That Walking Round My House Tonight, I've Come to See Poor Mary Jane, Steps and Stairs, Creeping, Branding, O'Leary; <i>Otago</i>: Sir Roger de Coverley, Who's That Knocking at My Door. <i>(1981,History of Children's Play,231</i>)

### Spaniard

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a sharp-spiked native plant of spp. Aciphylla that grows in high tussock country.

See: giant Spaniard, bloody Spaniard, wild Spaniard

[NOTES: also wild Spaniard]

>  <b>W.H.S. ROBERTS</b> Writing of the Waimea Plain in 1856: - `The ground was well grassed, but the speargrass was too plentiful. The pasturage was very good. There was a good deal of scrub in the bends of the Mataura known as `wire plant' (Olearia virgata). There were also manuka and koromiko. Maori-heads, a kind of grass tree about three feet high, abounded in the swamps, and in some we saw toitoi grass and raupo. We did not pass any cabbage trees to-day ... we proceeded slowly through tomatakuru scrub, speargrass, Spaniard, snowgrass, and other native grasses ... we camped in a bend with good feed at the Elbow and a swamp on one side. Maori cabbage abounded ...' <i>(1856,Diary</i>) [NOTES: 1856 W.H.S. Roberts Diary in 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 18]

>  <b>PAUL</b> <i>Aciphylla squarrosa</i> spaniard <i>(1857,Letters from Canterbury, NZ</i>) [NOTES: (And)]

>  <b>THOMSON</b> A new plant appeared here, allied to the cactus, and colonially termed a <i>`Spaniard' </i>It has stout blades with sharp points. <i>(1857,Southern Districts of Otago,311</i>)

>  <b>BUTLER</b> ... the sluggish creeks and swampy ground thickly overgrown with Irishman, snow grass and Spaniard ... which extend on either side of the river for half a mile or more. ... I will now return to the subject of wild Irishman and wild Spaniard. The former is a thorny tree growing with ungainly unmanageable boughs sometimes as large as our own hawthorn trees ... <i>(Jun 1860,Forest Creek MS,40,1961</i>)

>  <b>BUTLER</b> [Wild plants] are few, and decidedly ugly. There is one beast of a plant they call spear grass or spaniard, which I will tell you more about another time. <i>(Mar 24, 1860,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,4/49</i>)

>  <b>BUTLER</b> The Spaniard (spear-grass or bayonet-grass) `piked us intil the bane... <i>(May 1860,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,5/72</i>)

>  <b>HAAST</b> After crossing a small stream ... we arrived at such an impenetrable thicket of `Wild Irishman' and `Spaniards', that ... we had at last to give up the attempt with ... hands and faces covered with blood. <i>(1848,Julius Von Haast,210</i>) [NOTES: 1862 Mar 31 Von Haast in 1848 Von Haast Julius Von Haast 210]

>  <b>VON HAAST</b> ... the gigantic Aciphylla Colensoi, the Spaniard or Bayonet-grass. <i>(1862,Geology of Westland,25</i>) [NOTES: [check against 1879 cit???]]

>  <b>TAYLOR</b> In the Middle Island ... a great proportion of the land ... is one grand plain of shingle scarcely covered with soil, and only supporting grass ... much inferior to that of the North Island, filled also with spiny bushes of the Tumatakura, and that singular family of plants, the Acifolia Taramea, commonly called Spaniards; . <i>(1868,Past and Present of NZ,202</i>)

>  <b>KENNAWAY</b> ... we struck up ... towards the [Canterbury] mountains, the country being all level ... with a strong growth of coarse tussocks, pampas-grass, snow-grass (similar to the pampas, but having a deep red tinge in the blade) and spaniard or spear-grass ... <i>(1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,40</i>)

>  <b>HAAST</b> Our road lay now ... across a grassy flat, mostly overgrown with the same dense vegetation met with on the banks of all our river-flats, namely the spiny Wild-Irishman, and the bayonet-like Spaniard (<i>Aciphylla Lyallii</i>). <i>(1879,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,124</i>)

>  [Fantastic names of plants] show the imagination running riot; they seem appropriate, though often it is impossible to give any definite reason for the name. ... `Spaniard' [like `Wild-Irishman' is] another name of unexplained origin. There seems even less connection between the human Spaniard and the vegetable spaniard than between the human wild Irishman and the vegetable wild-irishman; and the conjectured corruption `spine-yard', whilst improbable, is no more improbable than the fabled `Bill's-yard' as the origin of `billiard' <i>(1926,TrNZI,663</i>) [NOTES: Andersen Pop. Names]

>  <i>Spaniard, speargrass</i>.- Various species of <i>Aciphylla</i>. Plants with stiff sharp leaves like rapiers growing out thickly in all directions from the ground. They were thickest in the hills, but there were plenty on the plains before they were ploughed. Horses avoid them carefully, which makes riding through them unpleasant. There are stories of men falling off and landing on one. Shepherds use the flower stalks for torches when burning. In the 'eighties and 'nineties at Mount Peel they used to all the broader leaved sort Spaniards and the narrower <i>Speargrass</i>; but most people use both names indiscriminately. ([1898 Morris Austral-English]) `There is one beast of a plant they call speargrass, or Spaniard.' (Butler A First Year in Canterbury Settlement], p. 48). <i>(Dec 16, 1933,Press, The,21/241</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  <b>LEVY</b> ... shrubs common in the tussock zone: matagouri, native brooms, dwarf koromikos, monoao, sarmentose tutu, the grasslike spiky-leaved Spaniard, the harsh patotara, golden cottonwood, cushion-like pimeleas, and the low, matted, carpet-like growth of the scabweeds are characteristic of the low tussock country, ... <i>(1951,Grasslands of NZ,35,1970</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> <i>Spaniard, n.</i> a prickly bushy grass of New Zealand, <i>Aciphylla colensoi. </i> <i>(1898,Austral English,427</i>)

>  <b>KIRK</b> <i>Aciphylla Colensoi</i> spaniard <i>(1899,Students' Flora</i>) [NOTES: (And)]

>  ... tumatakuru, a small thorny scrub, one of the few deciduous plants of New Zealand, which Europeans nick-named `Wild Irishman', ... speargrass, or `Spaniard', as the stronger variety was called, ... <i>(1914,History of North Otago,4,1978</i>) [NOTES: 1906 W.H.S.Roberts in 1914 History of North Otago (1978) 4]

>  <b>LAING & BLACKWELL</b> <i>Aciphylla squarrosa (The Spaniard) </i>... Maori name <i>Kuri-Kuri</i>; Colonists' [local] name, <i>Spaniard or Wild Spaniard. </i> <i>(1907,Plants of NZ,320,1940 p. 339</i>)

>  <b>WILLIAMS</b> <i>kurikuri.</i>.. 2. n. <i>Aciphylla squarosa, spaniard, spear-grass. </i> <i>(1917,Dictionary of the Maori Language,185</i>)

>  One of the spiny plants native to New Zealand some of them very tall;also called `speargrass' <i>(1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),377</i>)

>  <i>Spaniard [=] blue Spaniard giant Spaniard Spaniard taramea</i> [s] ... <i>Spaniard</i> [s] <i>Aciphylla squarrosa </i>Forst. <i>Aciphylla subflabellata </i>Oliver <i>(1969,Standard Common Names for Weeds,72</i>)

>  SPANISH CREAM - One and a-half pints of milk poured on  1/2oz of gelatine, to soak one hour, three eggs and four tablespoonfuls sugar; beat sugar and yolks together and pour in boiling milk; let it boil one minute, then pour this mixture on whites of the eggs which have been previously well beaten and placed in the mould. ### Spanish prisoner

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>BELTON</b> The [confidence trick] probably best known ... is the `Spanish Prisoner' ... [A letter is written to the victim ... intimating that the writer is prisoner in gaol and has a sum of money hidden, which he can get if he has ready cash to bribe warders and get out. He asks the victim for money to do this, promising to return it with a bonus.] <i>(1939,Outside the Law,142</i>)

### Spanish windlass

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <i>Spanish windlass</i>.- A contrivance for straining wire fences. It was cheap, easy to use and light to carry, but when wire-strainers were much im- proved early in this century it went out of use. At least, I haven't seen one for five and twenty years.
